          Causal Inference for a Universal Bank
Mathematical foundations and the construction of a shared product


                Research monograph and product proposal

Reader’s contract

Chapter 56 derives a restricted independent-pilot learning construction with explicit nuisance
error, finite dependent evaluation and weak-instrument sets. Exact references support the
derivation; useful precision and a fresh qualification study remain open. Section 43.12 reports
98 registered local workflow calls, preserving graph ambiguity, refusals, artifact failures and
restart identity. This does not install a discovery engine or establish live-model performance.
   Section 19.7 compares nine Python discovery families, with exact funding-direction,
observational-equivalence, numerical and selection examples. These are primary-source
comparisons and project calculations; downloaded engines were not executed, and broader
search and delegated-wrapper gaps remain explicit.
   Section 23.14 compares commercial latent-model fitting, clustering and trial-specific causal
effects. It develops hidden-risk and compliance examples and distinguishes these operations
from causal discovery under hidden confounding. Vendor capabilities are documented, not
executed here.
   Chapter 54 develops finite-table servicing-policy inference with estimated action and observa-
tion probabilities, independent evaluation, and explicit selection targets. Exact counterexamples
preserve the hidden-information obstruction; the finite guarantee can be too wide for a useful
choice. No new repeated-sampling qualification is claimed.
  Section 40.11 develops a restricted Python identification adapter, with exact positive and
negative references and a source-level conditional-identification counterexample. The proposed
workaround preserves the conditional query; no downloaded engine was executed.
   Chapter 53 derives a finite confidence region for persistent audits under explicit nuisance
bounds and an information limit for unrestricted calendar persistence. It preserves the
possibility of unbounded results and the earlier adverse findings; no new qualification study is
claimed.
  Section 23.10 compares documented GeNIe/SMILE and BayesiaLab paths with the proposed
product, including graph ambiguity, interface semantics and deployment rights. Stata’s
supplied-model SEM path is kept distinct. This bounded comparison leaves unavailable vendor
sources and unexecuted commercial trials explicit; it does not complete the commercial survey.
   Chapter 18 develops the survey method and a common causal software contract. It
compares five documented R paths, derives exact examples of graph and target ambiguity,
and specifies the proposed R and optional DoWhy boundaries. The algebraic examples have
been reproduced; the new package paths remain source-reviewed designs rather than executed
integrations. Section 31.10 extends the business-formulation discussion with seven primary
studies, three candidate package paths and an exact example distinguishing population,
trimmed and overlap-weighted effects.
   The immediate deliverable is a product proposal and bounded prototype evidence. Public
financial observations, experimental benchmarks and clearly identified synthetic mechanisms
can establish technical merit before costly bank experiments. Chapters 58–61 add a systematic

24-family dataset survey, six focused study families and a value-of-information argument. They
include a newly executed public bank-data profile; the proposed studies are not presented as
completed experiments.
   References elsewhere in this book to authentic bank truth, independent product acceptance,
production interfaces and measured bank ROI describe later conditional qualification. They are
not prerequisites for completing this proposal. The software, language-model and integration
repairs remain open. Current local demonstrations and public data support only their explicitly
stated claims.
   This integrated working edition contains the developed software comparisons, eight draft
chapters on language models and agents, and four draft chapters on library, command-line,
MCP and workspace integration. They form part of this book’s continuous argument, contents
and references. The source-audited earlier foundations and four scientific extensions are
retained, including negative calibration and qualification findings. The original delivered PDFs
remain separately preserved.
   This revision adds source-grounded comparisons of functional discovery, symbolic identifi-
cation, estimating equations, longitudinal regimes, continuous doses and network allocation
policies. Worked examples extend the treatment of business translation, diagram ambiguity
and evaluation. These are developed comparisons and exact illustrative calculations; the newly
inspected packages have not been benchmarked here.
   The systematic software survey, full depth of the language-model treatment, commercial
comparison, cross-language adapters and consumer qualification are unfinished. Local interface
demonstrations and exact project examples are not live model evaluations or accepted bank
integrations. This working edition has compilation, source-identity and extracted-text checks;
final rendered visual review remains pending. It is not the final repaired release or an accepted
bank product.
   A causal product must preserve a chain of reasoning. A bank defines a feasible intervention
and a population. A scientific model describes what that intervention changes and what
information the bank observed. Identification then either expresses the requested counterfactual
through the observed law, or explains why several answers remain possible. Only after that
step do estimation, machine learning and computational scale enter the argument.
   This manuscript reconstructs that chain. Its running example separates a randomized
invitation, actual product receipt, subsequent customer behavior, and the bank’s financial
outcome. The distinction leads to graphical identification and instrumental variables. Identified
functionals lead to influence functions, orthogonal estimation and heterogeneous-effect learning.
Repeated decisions lead to the longitudinal g-formula; partial observation then changes the
likelihood and the policy-evaluation problem. These are connected mathematical problems,
and the product’s interfaces must reflect the connections and the boundaries.
  The argument then develops econometric panels and structural shocks, causal discovery,
measurement and observation clocks, continuous-time models, policy learning, transport
and sensitivity. The software survey compares mathematical inputs and outputs before
proposing reusable operations, execution plans, banking studies and investment economics.
The companion sponsor proposal condenses the construction and investment decision; it does
not replace the assumptions in this monograph.
   Scope is explicit. The first product supports bounded identification and inference routes.
General nonlinear hidden-state identification, arbitrary network equilibrium and universal
inference for long dependent histories are not established here. The inherited 44-project
source/document survey, retained as a bounded baseline alongside the new pinned comparisons,
is supplemented by version-bound executions of selected numerical, columnar, DoubleML and
iv                                                            Causal analysis for a universal bank


Tigramite operations. The fitted comparisons distinguish calibrated examples from adverse
coverage and unavailable intervals; a supported likelihood is not automatically a qualified
confidence procedure. Local reference implementations connect observation construction,
inference and scientific result types. Read-only sibling API inspections and local mapping
examples establish a concrete integration design; accepted sibling adoption and a complete
bank workbench remain separate work.
   Every cited paper or book has a preserved PDF in docs/papers, a source identity and
hash, and inspected technical anchors. Source roles and remaining omissions are recorded
in the source–question matrix. The publication cutoff is 7 October 2026; acquisition and
inspection dates are retained separately. Coverage is a structured, bounded survey, not a
claim to have retrieved every relevant publication. Inherited results, project derivations,
finite counterexamples, fitted synthetic experiments and proposed behavior are distinguished.
Known-truth banking mechanisms are synthetic; archived household-finance and quarterly
monetary applications have unknown causal truth and explicitly qualified designs. Connected
funding and servicing constructions carry uncertain observations, learning and dynamic
dependence into reusable financial results. A linkage construction connects weak identification
to financial confidence sets, including disconnected and unbounded answers. The servicing
comparison separates public-history, private-state and audited-state information, and evaluates
a belief policy trained independently of its evaluation sample. Measurements include complete
reconstruction, fitting, uncertainty and reporting workloads as well as the earlier isolated score
reducer. The economic inputs remain planning assumptions. Neither the synthetic findings
nor the local timings establish bank adoption or enterprise performance.
   The bounded extensions distinguish persistent identity audits from correctness counts,
retain covariance and latent-graph uncertainty in outer effect sets, and develop an audited
nonlinear servicing likelihood with explicit policy and approximation comparisons. Separate
dependent-learning and restartable execution routes preserve their sampling experiments. A
completed calculation may still be uninformative or empirically unqualified; those outcomes
survive the public result rather than disappearing during monetary reporting.
   The reliability construction joins persistent pair audits to a common calendar under a stated
projection law and independent label validation. It derives finite Gaussian null-test effect
sets, extends one audited nonlinear transition variance model and fits a fixed richer dependent
dictionary through chunked QR. Fresh calibration and workload comparisons retain shortfalls
and small or absent cost advantages. Larger information designs provide bounded follow-up
evidence, while independent scientific, bank and platform acceptance remains separate.
   The funding calibration argument then derives the exact target shift from a finite independent
pilot and its required information growth. A fixed-regression alternative admits a two-pass
memory construction, while fresh comparisons retain its small-sample undercoverage and the
cost of a growing-pilot route. Improved attribution and local execution do not imply universal
calibration. A more precise comparison varies audit and pilot information and preserves
weak-information refusals. An equivalent streaming pilot retains chronological tuning and
monetary score inference; its storage benefit is qualified separately from coverage, elapsed time
and institutional adoption.

Chapter 1

Constructing a causal model and
identifying its questions

1.1     Begin with the intervention, unit and observation process
Consider a household eligible for a preferential deposit product. Let Z denote the bank’s
invitation, A actual activation, M a subsequent change in balances and Y the ninety-day
funding contribution. An intervention on Z is operationally different from forcing A = 1.
An increase in the database field recording A is different again. The bank can randomize
an invitation; it cannot generally compel activation or create liquidity merely by changing a
recorded balance. A causal question must identify the mechanism that the proposed decision
actually changes.
   The unit is a household rather than an account when money can move between accounts
owned by the same people. The outcome includes an agreed transfer price, interest paid and
servicing cost, with movements within the household consolidated. This is part of defining
Y , rather than a correction performed after estimating an account-level effect. For a fixed
population and horizon, write Y (a) for the outcome under a specified activation intervention,
and Y Z=z for the outcome under invitation assignment z. Two initial targets are

                     θA = E{Y (1) − Y (0)},        θZ = E{Y Z=1 − Y Z=0 }.                 (1.1)

They differ even in an ideal randomized invitation experiment. An invitation may have costs or
affect trust without activation. Such effects belong to θZ and threaten an exclusion restriction
used to infer θA .
  Consistency means that a household exposed to the specified action has its corresponding
potential outcome. It requires clarity about price, duration, channel, eligibility, execution and
outcome measurement. It is not ensured by giving all those interventions the same binary
code. Interference would require Yi (a), or a justified exposure mapping, instead of Yi (ai ).
The present single-period derivations assume a population of noninterfering units and a fixed
version of each action. Cluster or network designs must change those assumptions explicitly
(Hernán and Robins, 2020, Chapters 1–3).
  For clarity most graph calculations below use discrete variables and sums. Continuous
versions use conditional densities or probability kernels, with absolute continuity and inte-
grability stated at the estimation stage. This distinction matters: an intervention at one
exact continuous treatment value can be identifiable as a conditional-law functional without
admitting the same regular root-n estimator as a binary-treatment average effect.

2                                                                  Causal analysis for a universal bank


1.2     Structural equations supply the intervention semantics
Definition 1.1 (Acyclic structural model). An acyclic structural causal model M consists of
endogenous variables V = (V1 , . . . , Vd ), exogenous variables U , a joint law PU , and assignments
                              Vj := fj (Vpa(j) , Uj ),   j = 1, . . . , d,
whose endogenous parent graph is a DAG. A hard intervention do(A = a) replaces the
assignment for A by the constant a and retains the remaining assignments and exogenous law.

   The colon distinguishes an assignment from an algebraic identity that may be inverted
freely. A regression residual is constructed to be orthogonal to fitted regressors; a structural
disturbance represents omitted causes and need not be orthogonal to the action. Autonomous
mechanisms are what make intervention replacement meaningful (Pearl, 2009, Sections 3.1–3.2).
   If all Uj are mutually independent, the model is Markovian relative to its displayed endoge-
nous DAG. Hidden common causes can instead be displayed as latent parents, producing a
larger DAG, or left as dependence in PU . One must not draw an observed DAG and silently
assume independent disturbances after omitting a common cause. Both the functions and the
disturbance law are components of the causal model.
   Potential outcomes can be generated by recursively evaluating the modified assignments
at the same exogenous realization: Y (a) = fY (. . . ; a, U ). This constructs consistency and
expresses P {Y (a)} as the distribution of Y in the intervened model. Conversely, a potential-
outcome analysis need not posit mutually independent disturbances for every structural
equation. In particular, assumptions sufficient to identify each single-world intervention
distribution need not determine joint quantities involving incompatible interventions.
   The SWIG construction makes this distinction explicit. Split an action node into its random
part A, retaining incoming arrows, and a fixed part a, retaining outgoing arrows. Relabel its
descendants as counterfactual variables. For X → A, X → Y , A → Y this yields a graph for
(X, A, Y (a)) in which A ⊥ Y (a) | X can be read by separation. It does not simultaneously
supply a graph for the unobserved pair (Y (0), Y (1)). The SWIG framework covers the less
restrictive FFRCISTG model as well as the independent-error structural submodel (Richardson
and Robins, 2013, Section 2, node splitting and modularity). Consequently, identifying a
mean effect does not identify individual gains or their variance: Var{Y (1) − Y (0)} additionally
involves the unobserved Cov{Y (1), Y (0)}.


1.3     A diagram is constructed from mechanisms
Before drawing an arrow, define the decision clock. Here X is measured before invitation, Z is
assigned next, A records subsequent activation, M is later behavior, and Y closes the horizon.
Let U be unrecorded liquidity need and V a servicing difficulty that also affects outcomes. Let
C indicate whether the episode has a complete outcome record. A candidate mechanism graph
is shown in Figure 1.1. It is an assumption to be challenged with process owners and data
provenance.
   Each omitted arrow makes a substantive claim. Absence of Z → Y and Z → M says
that the invitation affects the economic outcome only through activation. Absence of causes
shared by Z and (U, X, V ) represents genuine random assignment in this example. Absence
of U → M says that liquidity need affects later balances only through activation or through
mechanisms already represented by X; this might be implausible and should be revised. A
discovered small regression coefficient cannot establish any of these omissions. Arrows allow a
mechanism; their presence does not prescribe its sign, magnitude, linearity or monotonicity.
1.4. Paths, colliders, latent variables and learned graphs                                       3


                                                  X




                              Z             A           M          Y



                                                  U


                                            C                      V

Figure 1.1: A proposed deposit-activation model. Dashed nodes are unobserved. The absence
of Z → Y encodes an exclusion restriction, while selection on a complete record C = 1 can
open A → C ← V → Y .


  A useful construction procedure has five concrete steps.
1. Define the actor, feasible action, unit, economic endpoint and clock. Separate assigned,
   received, recorded and measured quantities.
2. List causes of the action and of the endpoint, including private decisions, calendar conditions,
   common counterparties and selection.
3. Order mechanisms at the finest relevant time resolution. Replace apparent contemporaneous
   feedback by a justified within-period order or an explicitly cyclic/dynamic model.
4. Mark what is observed and when it becomes available; draw observation and inclusion
   mechanisms instead of treating missingness as a blank cell.
5. Examine every exclusion needed by the intended identification route. Record its business
   justification, plausible violations and what an experiment or additional measurement could
   resolve.
This procedure separates a causal diagram from data lineage. A lineage edge from transactions
to an aggregated balance describes a calculation. It does not mean that intervening on the
stored aggregate changes the underlying transactions. Deterministic accounting identities also
create conditional dependencies that require care in discovery algorithms relying on generic
faithfulness assumptions.


1.4     Paths, colliders, latent variables and learned graphs
A path ignores the direction of its successive edges. An internal node is a collider when
both adjacent edges have arrowheads into it. A DAG path is active conditional on S when
every noncollider is outside S and every collider has itself or a descendant in S. Two sets
are d-separated when no such path connects them. In a distribution Markov to the DAG,
d-separation implies conditional independence (Pearl, 2009, Definition 1). Faithfulness is the
additional converse assumption used by many discovery procedures; it is not needed to deduce
independences from a stipulated causal graph.
  In the bank graph, conditioning on X blocks A ← X → Y but leaves A ← U → Y open.
Adding M can block a causal path and therefore change the target. Conditioning on A opens
the collider Z → A ← U → Y : invitation and latent need need not remain independent among
activators. This is why analyzing compliance strata defined by observed receipt is not the
4                                                                          Causal analysis for a universal bank


same as randomizing receipt. Conditioning on C = 1 can also open A → C ← V → Y .
  For a numerical collider example, let A, V be independent fair binary variables, Y = V ,
and let C = 1 exactly when A = V . Action has zero causal effect on Y . Among records with
C = 1, however, Y = A, so the observed contrast is one. Positive marginal action probabilities
and perfect outcome prediction within the selected sample do not repair selection bias.
   Marginalizing latent nodes can yield an acyclic directed mixed graph (ADMG). In the
simple common-cause motif, A ← U → Y becomes A ↔ Y ; a directed latent path can induce
a directed observed edge. Directed and bidirected edges can coexist. The corresponding
separation rule, m-separation, uses arrowheads to define colliders in the same way. A bidirected
edge records a permitted hidden common-cause route; it is not an instruction to regress in two
directions. With selection and more general latent structures, maximal ancestral graphs and
PAGs require their own semantics; an ADMG is not interchangeable with those objects. The
latent-time-series setting of Gerhardus and Runge (2020, Section 2), for example, explicitly
excludes selection and targets a time-window-dependent ancestral equivalence object.
   A DAG supplied by an analyst, a CPDAG representing a DAG Markov-equivalence class,
and a PAG representing latent/selection-compatible ancestral graphs are different inputs.
For DAGs the same skeleton and unshielded colliders give the same implied conditional
independences (Peters et al., 2017, Definition 6.24 and Lemma 6.25). Two variables alone do
not observationally distinguish A → Y from Y → A. Known timing may exclude the latter but
still leave hidden confounding. A discovery score cannot turn the remaining graph ambiguity
into a unique causal effect by choosing whichever orientation permits an estimator to run.


1.5     Identification is a property of a model class
Let M be the class of causal models permitted by the assumptions, PM their observed-data
law, and θ(M) the requested effect. Identification means

               PM1 = PM2       =⇒      θ(M1 ) = θ(M2 ) for every M1 , M2 ∈ M.                             (1.2)

It permits writing θ = Θ(P ) for a statistical functional (Pearl, 2009, Definition 2). Identification
does not assert that the functional is well conditioned, estimable at root-n rate, or supported
with useful precision by the observed sample. Conversely, failure to find an adjustment set
does not prove nonidentification: another transformation may identify the target.

Proposition 1.1 (Truncated factorization for a fully observed Markovian DAG). Assume
independent structural disturbances, acyclicity and autonomous assignments. For a hard
intervention on a node set I, the density of the remaining variables is

                                 pa (v−I ) =          p(vj | vpa(j) ) v =a .                              (1.3)
                                                                       I
                                               j ∈I
                                                 /

Observed conditional kernels identify the right-hand side wherever the required parent configu-
rations have support.

Proof. Order nodes topologically. Independent disturbances imply that each assignment
generates a kernel conditional on its parents, giving the observational product j p(vj | vpa(j) ).
                                                                               Q

Replacing an assignment by a constant removes its kernel and substitutes its value in the
arguments of each child kernel. The other kernels remain invariant by autonomy. Iterating in
the same order gives Equation (1.3). Without support, a conditional kernel is not determined
by observational data at the parent configurations that the intervention creates.

   This is the causal Markov and truncated-factorization argument in Pearl (2009, Theorem
1 and Corollary 1). For a graph with hidden U , the full product may still be written and
integrated over U , but its factors involving U are not automatically observable. Replacing
them by conditionals of observed variables alone is an additional identification claim, not a
consequence of the chain rule.


1.5.1    Adjustment and its potential-outcome proof

Suppose a pretreatment set X blocks all paths entering A through an incoming arrow and
contains no descendants of A. The back-door criterion is a sufficient graphical route to
exchangeability in the stated model; it is not the most general adjustment criterion (Pearl,
2009, Definition 3). In potential-outcome notation the needed conditions for each action a are
consistency, Y (a) ⊥ A | X, and P (A = a | X = x) > 0 for almost every target x. Then
                                            X
                           E{Y (a)} =           E{Y (a) | X = x}p(x)
                                            x
                                            X
                                        =       E{Y (a) | A = a, X = x}p(x)
                                            x
                                            X
                                        =       E[Y | A = a, X = x]p(x).                   (1.4)
                                            x

The first step averages over the target population; the second uses exchangeability; the third
uses consistency, with positivity making the conditional mean observable. The graph is one
justification for those equalities, not an alternative to them. For the bank graph containing
A ← U → Y , X alone does not justify the second step.
  If instead all common causes are measured in X and the mediator has the law p(m | a, x),
the total-effect mean is     X
                                 E[Y | a, m, x]p(m | a, x)p(x).
                                  x,m

The mediator distribution must change with a. Regressing on M and reading off an action
coefficient while holding M fixed generally answers a different question. The difference is
visible before choosing a regression family.


1.5.2    Front-door identification when adjustment fails

Consider the distinct graph A → M → Y with a hidden common cause of A and Y , no direct
A → Y , no confounding of A → M , and all back-door paths from M to Y blocked by A.
Assume the required p(a, m) support. Under these restrictions,

                                                                    p(y | m, a′ )p(a′ ).
                                            X                  X
                          p(y | do(a)) =            p(m | a)                               (1.5)
                                                m              a′

To see the steps, A → M is unconfounded, so its interventional law is p(m | a). Setting M = m
cuts the incoming A → M edge; adjustment by A identifies p(y | do(m)) as the inner sum.
In this graph intervening on A changes Y only by changing M ; the response kernel under
an intervention on M is invariant to that A intervention. Composing these two intervention
kernels gives the displayed expression. It is not ordinary adjustment for a post-treatment
covariate (Peters et al., 2017, Section 6.7, Example 6.46).
  For deposits, measured balance change is rarely a defensible front-door mediator: liquidity
need may directly affect it and funding contribution may have activation-related cost channels
outside balances. The formula is useful because it states which measurements and exclusions
would be needed. It must not motivate deleting inconvenient arrows from Figure 1.1.
6                                                               Causal analysis for a universal bank


  Do-calculus generalizes these transformations by conditions for deleting observations, ex-
changing actions and observations, and deleting actions in modified graphs. For example,

                 p(y | do(a), z, x) = p(y | do(a), x)   if Y ⊥G Z | A, X in GĀ ,

where GĀ removes edges entering A and the separation statement is evaluated in that modified
graph. The action/observation exchange rule requires a different modification, removing
outgoing edges of the variable being exchanged. A compiler must retain the actual rule and
separation witness for each step. The next subsection explains how an identification algorithm
organizes such operations and distinguishes a failed search from a proof of nonidentification.


1.5.3    District decomposition and an obstruction certificate

In a semi-Markovian ADMG a district is a maximal set joined by bidirected paths. A singleton
without a bidirected neighbor is also a district. For S ⊆ V , define the interventional kernel
Q[S] = p(s | do(v \ s)). It is a function of s and the fixed outside values; in general it is not
the ordinary conditional p(s | v \ s). Shared hidden disturbances couple variables within a
district. Integrating over distinct independent latent groups factorizes an intervention kernel
over districts in its remaining graph.
   The ID algorithm exploits this decomposition recursively. With no intervention it marginal-
izes the supplied law. It first restricts to ancestors of the requested outcome, summing
irrelevant variables. It can then add interventions on remaining nonancestors in the graph
with the original intervention nodes removed, because they cannot change the target in that
graph. When the remaining graph has several districts, it identifies their kernels separately,
multiplies them, and marginalizes nonoutcome variables. When one district remains, it either
extracts topologically ordered conditional factors for a district already available in the current
kernel, recurses inside a larger containing district, or returns a failure witness. These steps
are made precise in Shpitser and Pearl (2006, Section 4, Figure 2); they apply to its specified
semi-Markovian model class.
   The obstruction is a hedge. An R-rooted C-forest is a bidirected-connected subgraph whose
observed nodes have at most one directed child, with childless root set R. Two such forests
F ′ ⊂ F form a hedge for the query when F meets the intervention set, F ′ does not, and their
common roots are ancestors of the outcome in the intervened graph. The source proves that
such a pair witnesses nonidentification and establishes completeness of ID for the specified
queries. These are inherited theorems; the following small case makes their practical meaning
concrete.
   For the bow graph A → Y , A ↔ Y , take F = {A, Y } and F ′ = {Y }, with common root Y .
The larger forest contains A and the smaller does not. Thus failure to identify p(y | do(a)) is
certified, rather than merely caused by a search routine finding no adjustment set. Section 1.6
constructs two positive observed-law examples witnessing that same failure. The front-door
graph avoids this obstruction for the total effect through an identifiable composition of district
kernels.
   Conditional interventional queries require another distinction. Dividing an identified p(y, z |
do(a)) by its z margin works when that joint law is identified and the denominator is positive,
but failure to identify the joint law need not settle the conditional query. The IDC algorithm
first exchanges eligible conditioning variables for interventions using do-calculus, then invokes
ID and normalizes the remaining joint kernel (Shpitser and Pearl, 2006, Section 5, Figure 3).
Its input is a conditional interventional distribution, not a generic cross-world mediation or
personalized counterfactual request.
1.5. Identification is a property of a model class                                               7


1.5.4    A recursive call trace, including a conditional rescue

The front-door functional can now be reconstructed as an execution of ID, rather than supplied
as a memorized template. Use the topological order (A, M, Y ) in the three-node front-door
graph above. The original districts are {A, Y } and {M }. Write ID(B, I; K, G) for a call
identifying the law of B after setting I, from the supplied kernel K and graph G. The line
numbers below refer to Shpitser and Pearl (2006, Figure 2).
1. In ID(Y, A; p, G), all nodes are ancestors of Y . Removing A leaves districts {M } and {Y }.
   Line 4 returns m ID(M, {A, Y }; p, G)ID(Y, {A, M }; p, G).
                    P

2. For the first factor, ancestor reduction (line 2) restricts the graph to {A, M } and the input
   to p(a, m). The intervention set becomes {A}. In this graph {M } is an original district;
   line 6 extracts p(m | a).
3. For the second factor, the remaining singleton {Y } is contained in the larger original district
   {A, Y }. Line 7 recurses inside that district with intervention A and kernel

                                     q(a, y | m) = p(a)p(y | a, m).

   This is a normalized kernel with m fixed. It is generally different from p(a, y | m) because
   p(a | m) ̸= p(a).
4. The induced graph on {A, Y } has a bidirected edge and no directed edge. Its ancestors of
   Y are just {Y }. Line 2 therefore marginalizes a, leaving qY (y | m) = a′ p(a′ )p(y | a′ , m)
                                                                           P

   and an empty intervention set. Line 1 returns that kernel.
5. Multiplication and the final sum over m recover Equation (1.5). The dummy a′ in the
   second kernel is distinct from the intervention value a in the first.
For a fully specified finite check, let U be fair binary and use independent innovations with
probabilities

 P (A = 1 | U ) = .2 + .6U,    P (M = 1 | A) = .1 + .7A,     P (Y = 1 | M, U ) = .1 + .5M + .2U.

All observed cells are positive. Direct intervention gives E[Y (a)] = .25 + .35a, while the
observed regression gives E[Y | A = a] = .19 + .47a. Enumerating the latent law and evaluating
the ID expression agree on the effect .35; direct adjustment for no covariates produces .47.
The numerical check validates this supplied example and its algebra, not an implementation of
general ID.
   A second graph shows why IDC has a separate role. Let A → M → Y and A ↔ M ,
with no other edges. The joint p(m, y | do(a)) is not identifiable: marginalizing an identified
joint would identify p(m | do(a)), contradicted by the bow-graph hedge on {A, M }. Yet the
conditional is identified. In GĀ,M , where incoming edges to A and outgoing edges from M are
removed, Y is separated from M given A. IDC line 1 exchanges the observation of M for an
action:
                              p(y | do(a), m) = p(y | do(a), do(m)).
ID then extracts the original singleton district {Y }, giving p(y | a, m) = p(y | m). Positivity
is still required at the conditioning value. Normalizing a failed joint-identification result
would have missed this valid conditional query. Conversely, the result does not identify the
distribution of M under the action or the unconditional action effect. This trace exemplifies
the distinction in Shpitser and Pearl (2006, Figure 3 and Theorems 7–8).
   An identification compiler should therefore carry typed kernels and intervention sets through
each transformation. Multiplying a district kernel as if it were an ordinary regression conditional
is a semantic error even if the expression is numerically evaluable. A graph outside the supported
class should produce an unsupported-method result; an actual hedge or paired-model witness
supports nonidentification.

1.6     Two observationally identical worlds
Here is a strictly positive counterexample adapted as a project derivation to the identification
definition. In model I, U is a fair binary variable, P (A = 1 | U ) = 0.2+0.6U , and, independently
of the action noise, P (Y = 1 | U, A) = 0.2 + 0.6U . Action has no effect. In model II, A is
independent and fair, with P (Y = 1 | A) = 0.32 + 0.36A. Both yield
                                           Y =0 Y =1
                                     A = 0 0.34  0.16
                                     A = 1 0.16  0.34
because, for instance, model I gives P (A = 1, Y = 1) = 12 (0.22 + 0.82 ) = 0.34. Their ATEs are
zero and 0.36, respectively. A class allowing hidden A/Y confounding and an action effect
contains both models. Its observed law therefore fails Equation (1.2). More data can estimate
the common table accurately but cannot choose between the intervention distributions.
   One can still describe an identified set. For binary Y , under consistency alone, let qa =
P (Y = 1, A = a) and pa = P (A = a). The unobserved part of E[Y (a)] lies between zero and
1 − pa , so
                              θA ∈ [q1 − q0 − p1 , q1 + p0 − q0 ].                       (1.6)
These elementary bounds follow by assigning the missing binary potential outcomes to their
extremes; simultaneous assignments attain the endpoints under the unrestricted consistency
model. For the table above they are [−0.32, 0.68]. They do not encode an IV, monotonicity
or substantive confounding sensitivity restriction. Adding one of those assumptions means
optimizing over a smaller, explicitly stated model class.


1.7     Selection, mediation and the population being answered
Suppose C = 1 marks observed outcomes. If Y ⊥ C | A, X and π(a, x) = P (C = 1 | A =
a, X = x) > 0, and X and A are observed for the full target cohort, then
                                                          CY
                                                                   
                                 E[Y | a, x] = E                 a, x .
                                                         π(a, x)
The identity follows by conditioning on Y, A, X and canceling π. It can be combined with
Equation (1.4) only if the causal adjustment assumptions also hold. If servicing difficulty V in
Figure 1.1 affects both completeness and outcome, this conditional observation assumption
may fail. Conditioning on retention or survival does not automatically define an effect for the
original eligible population. When an endpoint is undefined after an event, an imputation rule
alone cannot make the causal target well defined.
   Mediation adds another distinction. A controlled direct effect compares E[Y (1, m)−Y (0, m)]
at a feasible fixed mediator intervention. A natural direct effect compares E[Y (1, M (0)) −
Y (0, M (0))]. The latter combines counterfactuals from incompatible worlds and requires
restrictions beyond those for the total effect. Under consistency, suitable support, and
assumptions implying Y (a, m) ⊥ M (a′ ) | X together with the required action and mediator
exchangeabilities, one obtains
                      E[Y (a, M (a′ ))] =         E[Y | a, m, x]p(m | a′ , x)p(x).
                                            X

                                            x,m

The cross-world independence is an additional assumption, not something proved by fitting
the two observed regressions. Treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounding invalidates
this simple construction. A single-world analysis and the stronger independent-error model
must therefore remain distinguishable (Richardson and Robins, 2013).
1.8. What the product is entitled to return                                                    9


1.7.1    Edge assignments and a single-world alternative

For the simple independent-error system M = fM (A, X, UM ) and Y = fY (A, M, X, UY ), with
conditional independence of the relevant disturbances given X, an edge intervention can send
a′ along A → M and a along A → Y . The resulting response is fY (a, fM (a′ , X, UM ), X, UY ).
Integrating the independent disturbances yields exactly the mediation functional above. This
derivation makes its stronger model explicit: splitting a node into different edge values is not
the same intervention as setting the single node once. A manipulation of a composite product
that changes only a pricing channel also requires the claimed separation of those mechanisms
to have operational meaning.
   Now introduce a post-action covariate L that affects both M and Y . The natural response
Y (a, M (a′ )) involves L(a) in the outcome path and L(a′ ) inside the mediator path. The
observed conditional kernels do not generally determine the joint law of these two counterfactual
values. The same node would have to transmit different versions of its history along its outgoing
paths; ordinary single-world g-computation does not supply that joint law.
   A feasible alternative can be defined by a new randomized mediator draw Ga′ from p(m |
A = a′ , X), conditionally independent of the customer’s other innovations given X. Under
action exchangeability, mediator–outcome exchangeability given (A, L, X), consistency and
the requisite cross-regime support, direct mechanism replacement identifies the project-defined
target
                                      E[Y | a, l, m, x]p(l | a, x)p(m | a′ , x)p(x).
                                   X
                  E[Y (a, Ga′ )] =                                                        (1.7)
                                  x,l,m

The proof is the sequential g-formula: draw X, let L develop under a, independently draw
the mediator from the stipulated baseline-conditional distribution, then apply the invariant
outcome kernel. This intervention requires no joint (L(a), L(a′ )) law. It can be unrealistic if
the drawn mediator is infeasible for the resulting L, so support and operational feasibility
remain essential.
   Differences between (a, a′ ) pairs decompose effects of these new interventions. They do
not automatically decompose the original total effect: even Y (a, Ga ) can differ from Y (a)
because the fresh draw removes the natural association between L and M . For example, if L
is fair binary, M = L and Y = LM , the natural mean is 1/2 while independently drawing G
from the same binary margin gives 1/4. This algebraic example explains the target difference;
it does not satisfy mediator support for estimating the randomized intervention from that
deterministic observational law. Stochastic mediator policies conditional on the realized L
define yet another target. A product must preserve the chosen mechanism and conditioning
information instead of returning all of these as one “indirect effect.”


1.8     What the product is entitled to return
The mathematical input is an intervention, target population, observed information and
model class. Its identification output is either a functional with an assumption-dependent
derivation, a set of possible values, or a demonstrated failure of identification. A missing
software implementation is a fourth state: it says nothing about identification.
  For the graph in Figure 1.1, a result cannot be labeled “adjusted ATE” after simply fitting Y
on (A, X). A valid result might instead report the randomized invitation effect, the consistency
bounds, or an IV analysis with extra assumptions. If multiple candidate graphs remain,
compute the effect for each supported graph or carry their union of identified sets. Reporting
the spread across two handpicked graphs is only a sensitivity exercise for those graphs, not a
confidence interval covering all plausible causal structures.
10                                                         Causal analysis for a universal bank


   The initial product can implement explicit DAG back-door checks and registered functional
templates with human-supplied assumptions. It should record variable meanings, graph version,
intervention transformation, required kernels, support restrictions and target population
weights. Discovery and automated data preparation can propose inputs to this process; they
cannot certify the absence of unmeasured causes. The next chapter shows why an instrumental-
variable route changes the returned object even when it uses the same customers, actions and
outcomes.

2.1     Why an invitation is not an adjustment covariate
Suppress X, M, C temporarily and consider Z → A → Y with A ← U → Y . In a randomized
invitation study, Z changes receipt while U confounds receipt and outcome. The graph
expresses that Z is independent of the common causes and that all directed paths from Z to Y
pass through A. Neither condition is equivalent to Z ⊥ Y | A: conditioning on receipt opens
the collider path through U . An empirical association between Z and Y among activators is
therefore not by itself evidence against exclusion.
   The graph alone does not generally identify E[Y (1) − Y (0)] (Pearl, 2009, Section 3.5). Linear
homogeneous effects, monotone binary compliance, and a nonparametric structural response
each add different restrictions. This chapter develops the first two and connects them to the
inverse problem that arises in the third. Calling all three outputs an “IV effect” would lose
the scientific distinction.

and the conditional disturbance restriction are assumptions. A structural common cause of A
and Y allows E[ε | A, X] ̸= 0. The linear example in Angrist et al. (1996, Section 2) starts
from precisely this distinction between endogenous receipt and exogenous assignment.
   Let r(X) = E[A | X], ℓ(X) = E[Y | X] and m(X) = E[Z | X]. Iterating the conditional

   Compliance strata refer to joint receipt potentials, not observed groups. An observed

from expanding the product to all eligible households.

2.3.1       A constructive failure to identify the population ATE

Take 40% compliers, 30% always-takers and 30% never-takers, with fair randomized Z. Among
compliers set (Y (0), Y (1)) = (0, 1). Always-takers have observed Y (1) = 1; never-takers have
observed Y (0) = 0. Consider two completions of their missing potential outcomes:

              Stratum        Completion I (Y (0), Y (1)) Completion II (Y (0), Y (1))
              Complier                  (0, 1)                            (0, 1)
              Always-taker              (1, 1)                            (0, 1)
              Never-taker               (0, 0)                            (0, 1)

Both satisfy exclusion and monotonicity and yield the same full observed law of (Z, A, Y ):
receipt rates are 0.3 and 0.7, with Y = A. The first stage and reduced form are both 0.4, so
LATE is one. But the ATE is 0.4 in completion I and one in completion II. The observed IV
experiment cannot distinguish them. This is a project counterexample, not an appeal to a
generic statement that “IV has limitations.” It identifies the exact missing outcomes that a
population effect requires.

unqualified population ATE.

consequence of the compliance decomposition, not a generic extrapolation guarantee.

financial confidence sets from candidate responses and audit counts, retaining rank failure and
disconnected answers.

The instrument may be strongly predictive and precisely estimated while the exclusion is false.
A direct invitation effect of 0.02 outcome units produces bias 0.05 when π = 0.4, but bias 1
when π = 0.02. Weakness amplifies a small violation. An overidentification test can reject a
joint set of restrictions; failure to reject does not prove that all instruments satisfy exclusion,
especially when violations are shared.
   For a declared sensitivity range |δ| ≤ d in this scalar model, the admissible coefficient
interval is centered at the covariance ratio with radius d/|π|, before sampling uncertainty is
added. That interval comes from a substantive bound on a direct effect, not from a diagnostic
threshold chosen by software.


2.5     Machine learning enters after the moment restriction
For Equation (2.1), use the score

             ψ(O; β, η) = (Z − m(X)){Y − ℓ(X) − β(A − r(X))},              η = (m, ℓ, r).   (2.13)

At the truth its derivatives in arbitrary square-integrable nuisance directions vanish: an ℓ or r
perturbation multiplies a function of X by Z − m(X), whose conditional mean is zero; an m
perturbation multiplies a function of X by ε, whose conditional mean is zero. The derivative
in β is −κ, which must still be bounded away from zero for conventional strong-identification
inference. This is the partially linear IV score of Chernozhukov et al. (2018, Section 4.2,
Equations (4.5)–(4.8)).

  Estimate m, ℓ, r on other folds, evaluate residual products on the held-out units, and solve
the sample moment. The nuisance contribution to its population bias is

                                    b − m){(ℓb − ℓ) − β(rb − r)}],

because the first-order terms have zero expectation. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds this by a product
of nuisance errors. The useful ML rates are therefore rates for these moment errors and
the score variance, not merely predictive accuracy for Y . Dependence determines valid fold
construction and the CLT; arbitrarily splitting rows from the same customer does not produce
independent training and evaluation samples.


2.6       Control functions use a triangular structural restriction
There is another IV route that must not be confused with adjusting for an arbitrary first-stage
residual. Suppose

                    A = h(Z, X, V ),         Y = f (A, X, U ),         Z ⊥ (U, V ) | X,

where V is scalar, continuously distributed and h(z, x, v) is strictly increasing in v. Normalize
V | X to be uniform on (0, 1). Then the observed conditional rank

                                    R = FA|Z,X (A | Z, X) = V                                       (2.14)

almost surely. For fixed z, x, the event h(z, x, V ) ≤ h(z, x, v) is V ≤ v; independence of Z
proves the equality. Conditional on X, R, the dependence between U and the endogenous
disturbance is held fixed and the remaining action variation comes from Z, so U ⊥ A | X, R.
Consequently

             mcf (a, x, r) = E[Y | A = a, X = x, R = r] = E[f (a, x, U ) | X = x, V = r]

is identified on the joint observed support. This reconstructs Imbens and Newey (2002,
Assumptions 3.1–3.2, Theorem 1 and Appendix A), with observed covariates added by applying
the argument within their strata. Strict monotonicity in the latent rank is distinct from LATE’s
monotonic response to the observed instrument.
     To recover the average structural response at a specified a, one would integrate
                                             Z Z 1
                              E[Y (a)] =             mcf (a, x, r) dr dPX (x).                      (2.15)

This requires a to have support at almost every rank and covariate being integrated. The
source’s Assumption 3.3 and Theorem 2 make this additional support condition explicit.
First-stage predictability or rank recovery alone does not supply it.
  For an exact counterexample, let Z, V be independent uniform variables on [0, 1] and
A = Z + V . The two response systems

                        f1 (a, v) = a + v,          f2 (a, v) = a + v + c1{a < v}

agree on every observed record because A ≥ V . Both obey the triangular model and strict
first-stage monotonicity. Under do(A = .2), however, their average responses differ by .8c. At
A = .2 the observed ranks cannot exceed .2, while the intervention preserves all ranks. This is
failure of structural-response identification caused by support, despite knowing the control
exactly.
2.7. A nonlinear structural response is an inverse problem                                       17


  In the additive first stage A = πZ + V , with E[U | V ] = λV and Y = θA + U , regressing on
A and the true residual V is a sufficient special case. Outside it, a linear residual adjustment
can miss a nonlinear control function or fail because several latent dimensions determine action.
For discrete A, the conditional CDF is generally not an invertible latent rank. Estimated
ranks are generated regressors: inference must account for the first-stage CDF estimation and
any support trimming. The source’s two-step series estimator is one qualified route; it does
not establish validity for an arbitrary learned encoder called a control function.


2.7     A nonlinear structural response is an inverse problem
Suppose the model is Y = h(A, X) + ε with E[ε | Z, X] = 0. At fixed x the observable
regression g(z, x) = E[Y | z, x] satisfies
                                           Z
                          (Tx hx )(z) :=       h(a, x) dP (a | z, x) = g(z, x).              (2.16)

The operator Tx averages a structural response over the first-stage conditional distribution.
Identifying hx requires injectivity on its declared function class: Tx v = 0 must imply v = 0.
In unrestricted function classes this is a completeness condition, far stronger than a nonzero
scalar first-stage covariance. A binary instrument supplies only two conditional expectations
at a given x; those alone cannot identify an arbitrary function of continuous A.
  Even an injective operator may be ill conditioned. For a singular system T ϕj = σj χj with
small σj , inversion divides noisy coefficients by σj . Ridge regularization instead estimates
                                               X     σj
                                    hλ =            2     ⟨g, χj ⟩ϕj .
                                               j
                                                   σj + λ

It suppresses unstable directions and introduces bias. The formula is a direct singular-value
calculation; a full statistical NPIV survey must specify source conditions, estimation of T , rates
and uncertainty for the actual target functional. Deep networks are function approximators
inside this inverse problem; their expressiveness does not establish injectivity or valid exclusion.
Hall and Horowitz (2005, Sections 2 and 4) gives kernel and series estimators with rate
analysis for an estimated operator. Chapter 4 develops the distinction between function and
functional identification, regularization and proxy bridges, rather than treating inverse learning
as ordinary response regression.
   A control-function route uses different assumptions. If A = f (Z, X, V ) is strictly increasing
in scalar V , has continuous conditional distributions and (V, ε) ⊥ Z | X, then FA|Z,X (A |
Z, X) = FV |X (V | X) is a control variable. Conditioning on it and X can remove dependence
induced by V , subject to support and a suitable outcome structure. This rank construction
follows by applying the monotone inverse of f . Binary receipt does not have an invertible
rank of this form; inserting a binary first-stage residual into an arbitrary outcome model is
not justified by the argument.
  Proxy approaches solve related conditional expectation equations but assign different roles
to their variables. A variable measuring latent liquidity need can be a useful proxy while
being an invalid instrument because it predicts outcome through that need. Instrumental,
proxy, adjustment and learned-representation roles therefore require separate measurement
and exclusion assumptions. The theoretical survey must compare them at those restrictions,
not at their model architectures.

2.8     Result types follow the additional assumptions
The invitation experiment can return an intention-to-treat effect under randomization. A
homogeneous linear model can return a structural coefficient and moment-based uncertainty
under rank conditions. Monotone binary compliance can return a complier effect and its
population weights. An unrestricted IV graph can instead return bounds or an explicit
nonidentification result. A regularized inverse problem returns an estimate conditional on a
function class, operator restrictions and regularization.
   Each result must carry the original intervention, population, assumptions, first-stage evidence,
score or likelihood, dependence unit and uncertainty method. A weak first stage should
affect the inference state; a disputed exclusion should affect the causal assumption state.
Combining them into one opaque confidence score would conceal which remedy is required.
Additional randomization can improve support; a different encouragement may improve
relevance; measuring an omitted mechanism may alter the graph. None of these changes is
equivalent to running a more accurate predictor.
Chapter 3

Identification, statistical efficiency
and machine learning

3.1    Four different learning problems
Suppose Chapter 1 has justified adjustment by X. The observed data for an independent
household are O = (X, A, Y ), with binary A, propensity e(x) = P (A = 1 | X = x) and
response surfaces ma (x) = E[Y | A = a, X = x]. The scientific target is the population
average θ = E[m1 (X) − m0 (X)], or the conditional contrast τ (x) = m1 (x) − m0 (x). These are
causal targets only under the identification assumptions. The same formulas remain statistical
association functionals when those assumptions fail.
    Machine learning can estimate nuisance functions (e, m0 , m1 ), estimate the effect function
τ , optimize a policy using the estimated effects, or propose a causal representation or graph.
Each has its own loss and generalization question. An outcome predictor minimizes error for
observed Y under the historical action distribution. A policy learner values outcomes under
changed actions. The two losses are not interchangeable, and a random train/test split cannot
by itself bridge them.


3.2    Deriving an influence function for the identified mean
Work initially in an unrestricted dominated observed-data model with ϵ < e(X) < 1 − ϵ
and E[Y 2 ] < ∞. A regular parametric submodel Pt through P = P0 has mean-zero score

where E[SX ] = 0, E[SA | X] = 0 and E[SY | A, X] = 0. These are orthogonal score
components in L2 (P ), associated with the marginal covariate law, action mechanism and
outcome mechanism.

the bound; it is not automatically the bound for a panel with common shocks. Also, pointwise

additional structure or smoothing. A scalar ATE theorem cannot be used as a CATE
confidence-band theorem.

The assumptions are the substantive content of the DML guarantee (Chernozhukov et al.,
2018, Assumption 5.1 and Theorem 5.1); cross-fitting alone is not a theorem.
   Repeated records from one customer remain one dependent trajectory. Independent-
trajectory splitting holds out the entire customer. Common calendar shocks can couple
even different customers, requiring a different sampling theorem and covariance calculation.
For a single mixing time series, separated blocks may control training/evaluation dependence
under quantified mixing and gap conditions. A shuffled row split supplies no such argument.
The proposal must attach fold construction and the appropriate CLT to each estimator, rather
than expose a universal “cross-fit” switch.


3.4     Learning heterogeneous effects: compare the losses
The statistical CATE is a difference of response surfaces, but that does not determine the
best finite-sample estimation strategy. Several methods can target the same τ while exploiting
different structure.


3.4.1    Response models and imputed contrasts

A T-learner fits m0 , m1 separately. An S-learner fits a common regression m(a, x) and evaluates
its difference. Sharing parameters may help when arms are similar, but regularization can
suppress action interactions even when the factual prediction loss barely changes. A T-learner
can waste information when the arms share a complicated baseline but the effect is simple.
   An X-learner first fits both response surfaces and constructs Di1 = Yi − m     b 0 (Xi ) among
treated units and Di0 = mb 1 (Xi ) − Yi among controls. It then regresses those imputed contrasts
on X within their respective arms and combines the resulting effect regressions with a chosen
weight w(x):
                              τbX (x) = w(x)τb0 (x) + (1 − w(x))τb1 (x).
Imbalance can favor this construction if the larger arm estimates one response surface well
and the effect function is easier to learn. The weight is a statistical choice, not proof of
exchangeability (Künzel et al., 2019, Section on the X-learner).


3.4.2    Residual learning and its population metric

Let m(X) = E[Y | X] = m0 (X) + e(X)τ (X). Subtraction gives

                    Y − m(X) = (A − e(X))τ (X) + ε,          E[ε | A, X] = 0.               (3.4)

The R-learner minimizes a cross-fitted, regularized version of

                          L(f ) = E[{Y − m(X) − (A − e(X))f (X)}2 ].

At the true nuisances the cross term vanishes, so

                      L(f ) − L(τ ) = E[e(X)(1 − e(X)){f (X) − τ (X)}2 ].                   (3.5)

The loss concentrates information where both arms occur. Its curvature vanishes where
treatment is deterministic. The quasi-oracle analysis of Nie and Wager (2020, Sections 2 and
5) makes nuisance-rate and function-class conditions explicit; Equation (3.5) alone does not
establish a rate for an arbitrary neural learner.
22                                                                      Causal analysis for a universal bank


     If f is constrained to a constant, the target becomes

                                            E[e(X)(1 − e(X))τ (X)]

                                              E[e(X)(1 − e(X))]

which need not equal the ATE. For two equally common groups with effects 0 and 10
and propensities 0.5 and 0.01, respectively, the ATE is 5 but the residual-loss constant is
approximately 0.381. Neither estimate is a numerical error if it answers its specified projection
target. This target change must be visible in a product comparing a constant partially linear
model with heterogeneous effects.


3.4.3      Doubly robust pseudo-outcomes

The DR-learner regresses Φ(O)
                            b     from Equation (3.2), without subtracting θ, on X. At true
nuisances, E[Φ | X] = τ (X). With estimated nuisances, the conditional bias is exactly the
integrand of Equation (3.3). The second-stage regression can adapt to a simpler effect function,
but its error includes both that regression’s stochastic error and how it smooths the nuisance-
product bias. A product of global L2 errors sufficient for an ATE does not by itself guarantee
a pointwise CATE rate.
   Kennedy (2023, Sections 3–4) develops stability and oracle-error conditions for regression
with estimated pseudo-outcomes. That formulation clarifies why using an estimated outcome
is not a free replacement for observing the individual treatment effect. It also distinguishes
the second-order error of an orthogonal loss from the double-robust product structure of this
pseudo-outcome.

α/(2α + d) + β/(2β + d) > γ/(2γ + d). The analogous root-n average-effect argument needs

target x and do not establish the local premise.
   Oracle equivalence transfers an oracle inferential result only when that result is itself valid.
At a mean-squared-error-optimal bandwidth, smoothing bias can be of the same order as
standard deviation; inference may require bias correction or undersmoothing. Forest intervals,
kernel intervals and RKHS excess-risk theorems therefore need distinct guarantees. A score
being orthogonal is insufficient to label every displayed customer-level curve a calibrated
causal confidence band. Simultaneous coverage across many customer strata is an additional
uniform-inference problem.


3.4.5    Forests as local moment estimators

A generalized random forest constructs neighborhood weights αi (x) from tree leaves and solves
                         X                                         X
                               αi (x)ψ(Oi ; τ (x), ν(x)) = 0,           αi (x) = 1.
                           i                                        i

The score can be a local outcome, treatment or instrumental moment. Thus the same
computational architecture can estimate different statistical objects. Identification still depends
on which moment is supplied. Honesty separates observations used to choose splits from those
used to estimate leaf moments. Subsampling, regular splits, smoothness, local identification
and further conditions enter the forest CLT (Athey et al., 2018, Algorithm 1, Specification 1
and Theorem 5). Default forest fitting does not automatically establish all these assumptions,
and local weak instruments remain weak even when the forest predicts receipt well elsewhere.

3.5     Targeting, policy learning and the value of decisions
A one-step ATE estimate averages the augmented expression. A targeted substitution estimator
instead updates a fitted outcome regression so that its empirical score is close to zero, then
averages the updated contrast. For binary outcomes, one possible fluctuation is
                                                                              a     1−a
               logit ma,ε (x) = logit m
                                      b a (x) + εH(a, x),       H(a, x) =        −          .
                                                                            eb(x) 1 − eb(x)
The binomial likelihood derivative is i H(Ai , Xi )(Yi − mAi ,ε (Xi )). Solving it and taking
                                             P

θb = Pn (m1,bε − m0,bε ) makes the empirical influence-function mean zero for these fits. The
logistic map respects outcome bounds. This calculation explains a targeting step. Bernoulli
cross-entropy remains a valid mean loss for any outcome in [0, 1], even when it is not binary:
24                                                                    Causal analysis for a universal bank


its conditional expected derivative vanishes at the conditional mean. A financial outcome with
known fixed bounds can first be rescaled. Clipping an unbounded monetary outcome, however,
changes the estimand and cannot be justified merely to use a logistic implementation.
   To connect the update to inference, let m∗ denote the targeted fits and Φ   b ∗ their augmented
                                            ∗          ∗     ∗
expression. The solved score gives Pn Φ = Pn (m1 − m0 ) = θ. Consequently the expansion
                                          b                       b
is still the empirical true influence function plus the exact remainder of Equation (3.3), now
evaluated at m∗ , eb, and an empirical-process difference. The product-rate condition must hold
for the updated fits. If initial training uses separate folds but the fluctuation is fitted on the
evaluation observations, the final fits are not literally independent of those observations. Their
additional finite-dimensional dependence must be controlled, or a specified cross-validated
targeting construction used. The longitudinal construction and the score/remainder analysis
appear in van der Laan and Rose (2018, Chapter 4, Sections 4.4–4.5); its displayed Donsker
condition is one empirical-process route, not an automatic property of an arbitrary neural
learner.
   For a fixed binary policy d(X), and a per-action cost c(X) in the same units as the outcome,
incremental value over no treatment is
                            V (d) − V (0) = E[d(X){τ (X) − c(X)}].
Without capacity constraints the ideal rule is d∗ (x) = 1{τ (x) > c(x)}. A budget constraint
E[d(X)b(X)] ≤ B introduces a multiplier and changes the threshold to τ (x) > c(x) + λb(x)
under the usual separable relaxation. Optimizing an estimated score within a restricted policy
class differs from estimating a full accurate CATE surface: regret weights errors by their effect
on the decision boundary and by the policy restrictions. Policy evaluation and policy learning
therefore have distinct guarantees (Athey and Wager, 2021).
   If the same data choose the winning policy and produce its ordinary fixed-policy interval,
the interval does not account for selection. An independent evaluation sample, valid nested
splitting, or uniform policy-class inference is required. A model can rank policies usefully
without estimating every customer effect accurately, but a claim of positive incremental value
still needs uncertainty for the chosen decision procedure and the appropriate target population.


3.6     Representations do not manufacture an adjustment set
Suppose X suffices for exchangeability and a learned representation B = b(X) is proposed as a
replacement. A useful sufficient condition is that it also balances action: A ⊥ X | B. Indeed,
                              Z                                   Z
         P {Y (a) | A, B} =       P {Y (a) | x} dP (x | A, B) =       P {Y (a) | x} dP (x | B).

The first equality uses exchangeability given X and the fact that B is a function of X; the
second uses balance. Without that extra property a lossy representation can destroy the
identification route. The true propensity e(X) balances binary treatment because conditioning
on e(X) = b makes the probability of treatment the same b for every remaining X stratum.
An approximate learned score needs an estimation and overlap analysis.
   In the confounded two-world example of Chapter 1, use X = U as an actually observed
covariate. It permits adjustment. Mapping all X to a constant loses the distinction and
recovers a spurious contrast of 0.36. Adding an excellent predictor of a different component of Y
cannot restore the discarded confounder. Conversely, balancing representations cannot remove
an unmeasured common cause that was absent from the input. Distributional invariance across
environments needs assumptions about which mechanisms change; stable prediction in two
selected environments does not establish that an association survives an action intervention.
3.7. Consequences for the shared learning layer                                                25


3.7     Consequences for the shared learning layer
The product should accept an identified functional or moment, an explicit target measure,
nuisance roles and a sampling model. It can then choose compatible learners, splitting schemes
and uncertainty methods. The output must identify whether it is an ATE, an overlap-weighted
projection, a CATE curve, a complier curve or a policy value. A response predictor can be
shared across applications without transferring the causal validity of any particular application.
   Diagnostics should correspond to the mathematics: nuisance residuals and support, score
stability, fold leakage, local moment rank, regularization sensitivity and policy-selection rules.
Predictive validation is useful for nuisance fit; it cannot certify exchangeability, instrument
exclusion, causal representation or transport to another bank. These distinctions also determine
what automated data organization is allowed to discard or aggregate. The next chapter develops
inverse learning with endogeneity and proxies. Chapter 5 then makes the information set
dynamic and shows why sequence prediction is still only one part of the causal problem.
Chapter 4

Learning with endogeneity: inverse
problems and proxy bridges

4.1     Which object needs to be recovered?
The invitation experiment may identify a linear coefficient or a complier mean. A bank
asking how funding contribution changes over a continuum of deposit prices poses a different
question. Prices can respond to latent liquidity demand, so a flexible regression of contribution
on price learns the historical conditional mean, not automatically the structural response.
Equation (2.16) instead uses an exclusion and conditional moment to turn that response into
an inverse problem. The same mathematical issue reappears when historical actions use an
unmeasured condition for which the bank has imperfect proxies.
   Suppress observed covariates temporarily. Let HA = L2 (PA ), HZ = L2 (PZ ) and T : HA →
HZ be (T h)(z) = E[h(A) | Z = z]. Conditional expectation is a bounded linear contraction.
Its adjoint is (T ∗ q)(a) = E[q(Z) | A = a], since
                            ⟨T h, q⟩PZ = E[h(A)q(Z)] = ⟨h, T ∗ q⟩PA .
The observed regression m(z) = E[Y | Z = z] obeys T h = m under the structural conditional
moment. Existence says that m is in the range of T for the chosen model class. Identification
of the entire response says that the kernel ker T contains only zero on the allowed difference
class. These are separate restrictions. Fitting an approximate solution is evidence for neither
without further analysis.

4.1.1    A target can be identified when the whole response is not

Suppose one solution h0 exists. In a linear unrestricted difference space all solutions are h0 + v
for v ∈ ker T . A linear target θ = ⟨ℓ, h⟩PA is therefore identified precisely when
                               ⟨ℓ, v⟩PA = 0 for every v ∈ ker T.                              (4.1)
This follows by subtracting the targets of two solutions; it is a project linear-algebra derivation
at a fixed observed law. If h is restricted by shape, bounds or a nonlinear model, the allowed
differences must be restricted as well. The same statement with the full linear kernel need not
be necessary in that smaller class.
  For a finite illustration let A take three values and let binary Z supply the two averaging

4.2.1    What a primary NPIV rate theorem actually assumes

Hall and Horowitz (2005, Section 2.1) works with a positive integral operator formed from the
joint density of an endogenous regressor and instrument. Their operator is a density-weighted
normal operator; it is not literally the conditional-expectation operator T used above. Their
eigenvalue exponent α concerns that positive operator, and must not be silently read as the
singular-value exponent a.
28                                                             Causal analysis for a universal bank


  In their bivariate kernel result the observations are independent and identically distributed;
the regressor and instrument are supported on the unit square; their joint density has enough
bounded derivatives; and the relevant conditional second moments are bounded. In the
operator eigenbasis, response coefficients satisfy |bj | ≤ Cj −β , eigenvalues obey the lower decay
bound j −α ≤ Cλj , and joint-density coefficients obey the summability restriction in A.3. The
exponents satisfy α > 1, β > 1/2 and β − 1/2 ≤ α < 2β. With the density smoothness and
bandwidth restrictions in A.2, A.4 and A.5 and ridge an ≍ n−α/(2β+α) , their Theorem 4.1 gives
                                                                       
                                b − h∥2                   −(2β−1)/(2β+α)
                        sup EG ∥h     L2 ([0,1],dx) = O n                .                    (4.4)
                        G∈G

Here the source’s norm integrates with respect to Lebesgue measure on the unit interval; it is
not silently the earlier L2 (PA ) norm. The theorem handles an estimated operator; the sequence
illustration does not. The coefficient-decay condition gives a tail of order J −(2β−1) , which
explains why its smoothness notation differs from the ellipsoid exponent s. The separate series
result imposes a strong diagonality condition. None of these statements gives a confidence
band merely from choosing a ridge parameter, and the conditions cannot be transferred to a
bank panel with common shocks without a new sampling argument.


4.3       Proxy identification uses different exclusions from IV
Suppose U is latent liquidity need, X are observed pretreatment covariates, A is the bank’s
action, and Z, W are two sets of proxies. Here Z is not the randomized invitation of the earlier
example. Its reused letter denotes a treatment-inducing proxy; W is an outcome-inducing
proxy. A recorded private risk assessment may help predict U while failing to be an instrument
precisely because U also affects Y . Proxy identification can permit that dependence, but it
requires different exclusion restrictions.
  For each action a, assume consistency, positivity given (U, X), Y (a) ⊥ A | U, X, and the
proxy restrictions
                         Y ⊥ Z | A, U, X,     W ⊥ (A, Z) | U, X.
They can follow from a suitable latent DAG with no effect of A, Z on the pretreatment W
and no direct effect of Z on Y . Using a post-assistance balance as W would ordinarily violate
this restriction. The latent condition U must include the relevant shared causes; labelling two
arbitrary database columns as proxies does not establish it.
     Suppose a square-integrable outcome bridge exists satisfying

                        E[Y | Z, A = a, X] = E[h(W, a, X) | Z, A = a, X].                     (4.5)

Also assume latent completeness: for fixed a, x, E[v(U ) | Z, A = a, X = x] = 0 implies v(U ) = 0
almost surely in the relevant class. Define da (U, X) = E[Y | U, A = a, X]−E[h(W, a, X) | U, X].
The exclusions and bridge equation give E[da (U, X) | Z, A = a, X] = 0. Completeness makes
da = 0. Consistency and latent exchangeability then give

                       E[Y (a)] = E[E[Y | U, A = a, X]]
                               = E[E[h(W, a, X) | U, X]] = E[h(W, a, X)].                     (4.6)

This is a mean-level reconstruction of the proxy-identification argument in Miao et al. (2018,
Sections 2–3 and Theorem 1); observed covariates and the mean-bridge formulation are stated
explicitly in Ghassami et al. (2022, Section 4, Assumptions 4–6 and Theorem 3).
  Three restrictions must remain distinct. Latent completeness justifies the step from an
observable bridge equation to a latent causal equality. Bridge existence says that the observable
4.4. Two bridges produce a doubly robust estimating expression                                29


conditional mean lies in an operator range. Observable completeness of W given (Z, A, X)
can give uniqueness of h. A matrix rank estimated from proxies does not directly verify
latent completeness; moreover uniqueness of every bridge value is stronger than uniqueness
of its causal average. Miao et al. (2018) explicitly permits nonunique bridge solutions while
identifying the effect under the stated restrictions.


4.3.1    A finite banking construction with an exact answer

Let P (U = 1) = 1/2. Conditional on U , generate independent A, Z, W with probabilities of
one
          pA (U ) = 1/5 + 3U/5, pZ (U ) = 3/10 + 2U/5, pW (U ) = 1/10 + 4U/5,
and let Y = 2A + 3U . All combinations have positive probability. The causal effect is 2. The
raw treated-minus-untreated contrast is 2 + 3(0.8 − 0.2) = 3.8. Adjusting for a single noisy
proxy need not recover 2.
  The outcome bridge
                                  h(w, a) = 2a − 3/8 + 15w/4                                (4.7)
satisfies E[h(W, a) | U ] = 2a + 3U , hence the observable bridge equation. Since P (W =
1) = 1/2, averaging gives E[h(W, a)] = 2a + 1.5 and effect 2. The 2 × 2 matrix with rows
P (W = · | Z = z, A = a) is invertible in either action stratum, so this bridge can be recovered
from observed conditional moments without observing U .
   Now let W lose all information about U while retaining independent noise. Its conditional
rows become equal. Full column rank is lost and the bridge cannot reproduce a Z-varying
outcome regression. Replacing the inverse by a pseudoinverse returns a numerical vector, but
does not restore the missing equation or identify the original target. This is the proxy analogue
of a weak or unidentified IV direction.
