The finite recursion is the belief-state planning construction (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Four
signals, two actions and four decisions permit exact tree enumeration here. The tree is optimized
using an independent 2,000-trajectory audit pilot, then frozen in its entirety. Evaluation fits
kernels on separate audited trajectories and propagates their uncertainty through this fixed
tree. It differentiates neither the argmax nor the pilot training procedure. The interval targets
the value of the policy that was actually trained, conditional on that pilot, not the unknown
optimal value.
   To evaluate the fixed tree without numerical posterior divisions, propagate unnormalized
state mass. At each signal branch multiply by E·o , add the selected action’s expected reward,
and propagate through Ta . Summing all leaves gives a polynomial in the kernels and initial
law, linear in the rewards. Its derivative is therefore well-defined for the fixed tree; central
differencing is checked against a smaller step and independent likelihood/count perturbations.
Exact enumeration avoids a filter approximation error in this selected problem. Larger horizons
require pruning or approximate planning and an explicit value-loss bound.
7.13. A resolved information and inference design for servicing                                67


   On the common mechanism the frozen learned policy has true four-period contrast 25.029
against never assisting. Some actions depend on earlier signals even after holding the current
signal and remaining horizon fixed; this is a belief-history policy, rather than an immediate-
reward rule. At 1,200 audited evaluation trajectories, all 400 fits are available and coverage
is .950 for this contrast. The original eight-period fixed-signal contrast has coverage .9425.
At 300 audited paths, 54 of 400 fits have an empty category; all-request coverage is .8275 for
the learned policy even though coverage conditional on availability is .9566. Measurement-
supported identification therefore still requires enough informative visits.


7.13.4    Three information routes on the same servicing problem

An observed-history g-formula substitutes the factual conditional law given public signals and
actions. Under private logging its state posterior after action a is proportional to bo (s)qs (a),
while the intervention posterior is bo (s). Thus even an exactly estimated public-history
conditional law uses the wrong state mixture for the intervention. Adding a flexible learner
cannot remove this information gap. Recording the action-relevant private information,
or randomizing assistance with adequate support, changes that conclusion. The common-
mechanism comparison evaluates both recursions on the same frozen policy. Its exact public-
history g-formula contrast is −35.647, against the intervention contrast 25.029. The sign
reversal occurs even without nuisance estimation error.
   Validated emissions can identify the kernels using the earlier marked moment/hidden-
likelihood route, with fewer labels but difficult finite curvature and boundary behavior. Fully
audited trajectories identify the same kernels and policy target more directly, with the explicit
acquisition cost above. Their precision and availability are properties of different sampling
designs, not proof that hidden-state modeling is unnecessary.
   Proximal evaluation instead seeks policy value without recovering named states. For this
servicing mechanism an action-side proxy might be a separately recorded officer assessment, and
an outcome-side proxy an independent affordability measurement. Merely calling them proxies
proves nothing: after conditioning on the latent confounder and allowed context, the action-side
proxy and logged action must be independent of the outcome-side proxy, proposed action and
counterfactual continuation under the source’s hybrid laws. The proposed policy cannot reuse
forbidden private proxy information. Bennett and Kallus (2023, Assumptions 1–2, Theorem 2
and Table 1) give these policy-dependent restrictions and the recursive action/outcome bridges.
In particular their outcome bridge targets E[1{Et = At }Yt | Ut , At = a], where Et denotes the
proposed action; dropping that indicator changes the theorem.
  The source’s recursive bridge score is a substantive challenger when the bank can defend
those exclusions and bridge existence/rank conditions but cannot obtain accurate state labels.
The current production feed has one public signal stream and no independently validated second
proxy. It cannot invoke that theorem by relabelling the same signal twice. If an additional
proxy is collected, its conditional operator, range, regularization and policy information set
become new scientific inputs. This explains why the audited trajectory route is selected for the
bounded decision capability and proximal evaluation remains a qualified alternative, rather
than claiming that one existing dataset satisfies all three information regimes.


7.13.5    The initial product boundary

The offering includes finite-state estimation and observable-history policy evaluation under
a qualified measurement design, plus the earlier exact linear-Gaussian controlled likelihood.
It does not include arbitrary nonlinear private-state fitting with routinely calibrated policy
68                                                                                    Causal analysis for a universal bank


intervals. Choosing an extended Kalman or particle filter would require a declared likelihood,
initial/noise laws, derivative accuracy and policy-value comparison against a numerical reference,
following the approximation obligations already derived. Section 7.14 supplies a selected
audited nonlinear comparison with additional information and policy-class restrictions. Those
restrictions affect which bank requests can be accepted; they are not postponed as a generic
deployment check. A noisy or selected audit also changes the statistical model, even when
all matrices are well-conditioned. In a separately registered 200-repetition sensitivity run,
independently misclassifying 10% of predecision state labels at 1,200 audit trajectories produces
bias −105.72 for the original 59.56 contrast and zero coverage. This is a specific severe
misspecification example, not a calibrated bound for every 10% audit-error process.


7.14      An audited nonlinear servicing experiment
The exact Gaussian construction leaves a substantive question: what changes when the state
transition bends and a private binary decision reveals hidden state information? A small
servicing experiment gives a complete answer for one identified model. It also exposes the
difference between an accurate likelihood and a reliable routine interval.
  For each independent customer the order is state, signal, action, reward, then next state. In
units fixed by an accurate state audit, let

                             S0 ∼ N (µ0 , v0 ),                                                   Ot = St + et ,        (7.21)

      Pr(At = 1 | St , Ot ) = ϵ + (1 − 2ϵ) expit(λ0 + λs St + λo Ot ),
                            Rt = η0 + ηs St + ηa At + ηsa St At + vtR .                                                 (7.22)

Independent Gaussian innovations have positive variances q, ro , rR . Their log variances, both
initial parameters, three transition coefficients, three logger coefficients and four reward
coefficients give 15 unknowns. The fixed logger floor is ϵ = .05; stability requires |ρ| + |γ| < 1.
Rewards are in thousands of currency units. These are synthetic scientific restrictions, not a
fitted description of a real bank.


7.14.1      Identification comes from the observation design

Production observes (O, A, R); an independent representative audit observes complete labelled
(S, O, A, R) trajectories. The loading one in O = S + e and the labelled scale of S fix state
meaning. Under positive definite population Gram matrices, regressing St+1 on (St , tanh St , At )
identifies the three transition coefficients and its residual identifies q. The signal residual
identifies ro . Regressing reward on (1, St , At , St At ) identifies its coefficients and variance;
labelled initial states identify (µ0 , v0 ). The clipped logistic probability is strictly increasing in
its index. Equality of these probabilities on a full-rank support for (1, S, O) therefore implies
equality of the logger coefficients. The positive action floor supports both actions; full rank
and representative labels remain substantive requirements. This establishes identification
before filtering. Filtering does not create the audited states. Noisy or selected labels change
this argument.

seeds at 512 and 4,096 particles expose Monte Carlo variation. Coupled finite differences assess
stochastic likelihood perturbations; they are not a certified derivative through a discontinuous
resampling path. These are substantive alternatives to Gaussian projection, as emphasized by
Särkkä (2013, Chapters 6–7).

7.14.4    Boundary failures and a fresh information comparison

The first registered baseline uses 160 audits and 80 production trajectories, with |ρ| ≤ .55,
|γ| ≤ .4. Only 55 of 100 fits are interior; 45 hit a boundary. Of the 55 available intervals, 54
cover. Reporting only 54/55 would hide availability: coverage over requested calculations is
54/100. Misspecified transitions yield 25 unavailable fits out of 25. Weak signals, scarce actions,
biased audits and a six-date horizon are separate retained arms; successful optimization does
not validate their assumptions.
   A fresh registered comparison keeps the original policy and tests |ρ| + |γ| ≤ .95, each
coefficient in [−.9, .9], against the original rectangle. Other bounds stay fixed. With 160
audits the stable domain gives 99 available intervals and 94 covering draws out of 100. With
640 audits all 100 are available and 95 cover, with Monte Carlo interval [.8872, .9836]. Mean
standard error falls from about 168.06 to 95.84 currency units. The rectangular challenger is
available in 59 and 79 draws on these same designs. No result switches methods after observing
its interval.
  This supplies an identified and executed nonlinear reference, including a useful larger-audit
regime and explicit failures. It does not establish routine validity for arbitrary private-state
laws, erroneous audits, weak information, unrestricted policies or unknown global optimizer
behavior. Those require renewed scientific arguments and evidence.
Chapter 8

Panel data: heterogeneity, timing
and structural moments

8.1     Repeated measurements do not specify the identification
        strategy
A panel of branch deposits can support several different questions. One can model a homoge-
neous response to price after removing stable branch differences, identify an adoption-cohort
effect from untreated trends, fit an interactive-factor counterfactual, or estimate a dynamic
equation using lagged instruments. All use a rectangular data set; their counterfactual
assumptions are different.
  Let i = 1, . . . , N index branches and t = 1, . . . , T calendar periods. Write Yit (āt ) for the
outcome under an action history. The shorter Yit (at ) assumes away carryover. Let Gi be the first
adoption date only when an absorbing intervention makes that description meaningful. A price
that rises and falls, a repeated collections action and a permanent branch rollout do not share
the same treatment history merely because each is coded as a binary column. Arkhangelsky
and Imbens (2024, Sections 2–4) emphasizes assignment pattern, potential-outcome dynamics
and the relative sizes of N, T as distinct organizing dimensions.
  Banking measurements also change composition. Branch closure can remove a low-performing
unit, household transfers can move balances between branches, and a merger can change the
entity represented by an identifier. An unbalanced panel is not automatically missing at
random. The outcome and unit definitions of Chapter 1 remain part of the panel estimand.


8.2     Fixed effects remove a component, not all confounding
Consider the static linear structural specification

                                Yit = αi + λt + βAit + Xit′ γ + uit .                           (8.1)

The interpretation of β as a common causal response requires linearity, absence of omitted
carryover and an invariant outcome equation. A sufficient mean restriction for the within
estimator is strict exogeneity,

                             E[uit | αi , Ai1:T , Xi1:T ] = 0 for every t,

with common time components treated appropriately. This permits αi to correlate with the
entire action/covariate history. It rules out current shocks predicting future actions after

                                                  71
72                                                                 Causal analysis for a universal bank


conditioning on the specified regressors. For example, an unexpected deposit outflow that
causes next month’s retention offer threatens strict exogeneity, even if the offer cannot affect
past outcomes.
   For a balanced panel, two-way demeaning gives Äit = Ait − Āi· − Ā·t + Ā, and analogously for
Y, X, u. The stable branch effect and common time effect vanish. Frisch–Waugh residualization
by Ẍ then gives

Identification needs the numerator’s mean restriction and nonzero residual variation; the data

design matrices replaces this simple double-demeaning formula. Treating missing cells as zero
changes that projection.


8.2.1    Random and correlated effects change the restrictions

Random-effects GLS uses between-unit as well as within-unit variation. In the elementary
model with αi independent of regressors, Var(αi ) = σα2 and independent homoskedastic uit ,
the within-unit covariance is Ωi = σu2 IT + σα2 11′ . Its eigenvalue in the constant direction
is σu2 + T σα2 , and in the remaining directions it is σu2 . Hence, up to a common scale, GLS
quasi-demeans each variable as xit − ϑx̄i , with
                                               s

This project covariance derivation explains its efficiency gain under the stronger mean model
and its exposure to confounding between units.
    A correlated-effects specification instead posits, for example, E[αi | Ai1:T , Xi1:T ] = c +
δ Āi + X̄i′ π and adds those means to the regression. It permits a particular dependence on
histories while restricting its functional form. It does not make arbitrary adaptive assignment
ignorable. Nonlinear models also introduce an incidental parameter issue when one estimates
many unit intercepts with small T ; removing linear means is not a general nonlinear solution
(Arkhangelsky and Imbens, 2024, Sections 2 and 3).


8.3     Dynamics turn lagged outcomes into endogenous regressors
Consider
                              Yit = ρYi,t−1 + βAit + αi + λt + uit .                              (8.2)
Even if uit is a martingale difference relative to past outcomes, the within transform of Yi,t−1
contains earlier innovations also present in the within transform of the error. Differencing gives

                            ∆Yit = ρ∆Yi,t−1 + β∆Ait + ∆λt + ∆uit .

In the simplest case with no action, αi = 0, Yi0 = 0 and independent unit-variance ui1 , ui2 , the
two-period regression uses ∆Yi1 = ui1 and ∆Yi2 = (ρ − 1)ui1 + ui2 . Its population coefficient
is ρ − 1, not ρ. More branches do not remove this short-panel bias. This exact construction
illustrates the problem without claiming that its numerical bias formula applies at arbitrary T .
8.4. Difference-in-differences identifies an untreated evolution                                    73


8.3.1    The valid lag is determined by a moment restriction

If innovations are serially uncorrelated and initial observations are orthogonal to future
innovations, then for appropriate s ≤ t − 2

                                       E[Yis (uit − ui,t−1 )] = 0.                                (8.3)

By contrast, Yi,t−1 contains ui,t−1 and is not a valid instrument for the differenced equation.
For action regressors, strictly exogenous Ais can supply all date moments. Predetermined
actions orthogonal to current/future innovations can supply s ≤ t − 1; actions correlated with
current innovations require earlier valid lags, typically s ≤ t − 2 under the corresponding
sequential restriction. These are assumptions about the assignment/error clock, not a software
convention about lag length.
   Stack valid instruments in Zi and differenced structural residuals in ∆ui (θ), with θ =
(ρ, β, . . .). The GMM criterion is

This is the moment-estimation framework of Arellano and Bond (1991, Section 2, equations

main argument. Differenced white-noise innovations have first-order covariance −σu2 and zero
covariance at lag two; thus first-order correlation in differenced residuals is expected, whereas
a second-order correlation diagnostic probes a key validity restriction. The paper’s Section 3
derives the test and its estimation corrections. Failure to reject does not establish the exclusion
of a bank’s omitted policy response or measurement process.
   Persistent balances can make lagged levels weak instruments for changes. A large menu
of lags can also create many moments relative to the number of independent branches. The
weak-IV discussion then matters inside the panel estimator. Extra level-equation moments,
for example E[∆Yi,t−1 (αi + uit )] = 0, require additional initial-condition/mean-stationarity
restrictions; they do not follow from Equation (8.3). A product option that adds such moments
must expose those extra restrictions explicitly. Section 8.9 develops the additional initial-law
argument and GMM covariance, and distinguishes the implemented first-order sandwich from
an unimplemented finite-sample correction.

8.5     Staggered adoption requires explicit comparison groups
For absorbing adoption date Gi = g, define ATT(g, t) = E[Yit (g) − Yit (∞) | Gi = g]. With no

comparison horizon. These are the separate Assumptions 3–6 and identification routes in

8.6     Synthetic controls replace common trends by a factor re-
        striction
Suppose untreated outcomes obey Yit (0) = δt + λ′t fi + εit , with time-varying factors λt and

                        P

Exact loading balance removes the factor component at every time. In a noiseless model,
exact pretreatment fit identifies that balance only when the preperiod factor matrix spans all
relevant loading directions. A factor emerging only after rollout defeats that inference. This
algebra explains the factor-model motivation and convex-hull conditions in Abadie et al. (2010,
Section 2.2 and Appendix B).
   For example, donors with loadings 0 and 1 cannot convexly match a treated loading 2. An
unconstrained extrapolation can match it with weights (−1, 2), at a different variance and
robustness cost. A penalized augmentation can reduce imbalance under an additional outcome
model, while an interactive-factor estimator estimates factors and loadings directly. Those
choices exchange interpolation stability for model dependence; good pretreatment fit alone
does not choose between them. Donor contamination from a common promotion or balance
transfers also violates the required untreated donor interpretation.
  With one treated region, placebo reassignment describes an inference procedure only under
an appropriate assignment or exchangeability argument. It is not automatically an exact
randomized-experiment p-value. A historical fit across a handful of branches is likewise not
an independent sample of policy rollouts. The inferential regime must be stated with the
counterfactual model.

8.7     Uncertainty follows the independent information, not the

   Cross-fitting must respect the same structure. Holding out rows from a customer leaves

a held-out rectangle can train on observations outside both its row and column groups. The
multiway DML results of Chiang et al. (2021, Assumptions 1–3, Theorems 1–2) require
separately exchangeable, dissociated arrays, growing cluster dimensions, score regularity and
nuisance rates. Ordered banking time series need not be separately exchangeable across
calendar dates. Those theorems cannot be invoked for serial dependence merely because the
software accepts two cluster identifiers.


8.8     What the panel operation must declare
A panel request must identify whether it targets a structural coefficient, a cohort/time ATT, a
path contrast or a donor-based counterfactual. It must include the action’s reversibility and
carryover, the independent unit, the time asymptotic regime, the treatment/control support
and the allowed common shocks. Fixed effects, lag instruments, trend restrictions and factor
balance are alternative pieces of scientific evidence, not defaults inferred from the table’s shape.
   An eligible output preserves aggregation weights, unsupported horizons, instrument re-
strictions, donor contamination checks and the covariance construction. The bank can then
distinguish an effect that changes sign because of economics from a regression coefficient that
changes sign because it averages positive effects with negative weights. That distinction is a
prerequisite for financially meaningful cross-application reuse.

8.9     System moments, initial conditions and the practical panel
        choice
The difference equation removes an individual effect; it does not create a strong instrument.
This distinction matters for persistent loan balances or capital ratios. Consider first the scalar
model
            yit = αi + ρyi,t−1 + vit ,   |ρ| < 1, E[vit | αi , yi1 , vi2 , . . . , vi,t−1 ] = 0.
Independent entities and fixed T define the sampling experiment. For s ≤ t − 2, both E[yis vit ]
and E[yis vi,t−1 ] vanish, giving E[yis ∆vit ] = 0. These are the differenced moments already
derived above (Arellano and Bond, 1991). Their validity does not require the initial observation
to have the stationary distribution.
  Level equations permit a different restriction. Write yi1 = αi /(1 − ρ) + ei1 . Then

                  ∆yi2 = (ρ − 1)ei1 + vi2 ,         E[∆yi2 αi ] = 0 if E[ei1 αi ] = 0.

The recursion ∆yit = ρt−2 ∆yi2 + t−3     j
                                    P
                                    j=0 ρ ∆vi,t−j propagates this zero covariance. Consequently
E[∆yi,t−1 (αi + vit )] = 0. Combining these level moments with differenced moments yields
system GMM. Mean stationarity is sufficient for this construction; equality of initial and
limiting variances is not required. Conversely a portfolio assembled at loan origination or after
a balance-sheet repair may systematically start above or below its entity-specific long-run
level. The additional moment can then fail even when the differenced moments remain valid.
This reconstructs the initial-condition argument in Blundell and Bond (2023, Sections 3.1–3.3,
pp.107–109). The archived text is their 2023 account, not the original 1998 article.
   Adding βxit requires a separate classification for x. Contemporaneous endogeneity excludes
xit as an instrument; lagged levels must precede both innovations in ∆vit . Predetermination
and strict exogeneity allow different lag sets. A level moment using ∆xi,t−1 also needs
E[∆xi,t−1 αi ] = 0 and orthogonality to vit . No initial-condition theorem for y automatically
supplies this condition for a bank’s chosen action. With common macro shocks, cross-entity
independence itself fails and the fixed-T , large-N argument must change.

   Compression also changes a statistical problem. An unrestricted triangular lag matrix has
(T − 2)(T − 1)/2 instruments in the scalar differenced model. The reference collapses moments
over dates and keeps lags two and three, yielding four differenced moments for (y, x), or six
after adding level moments. Scaling moments by observed root mean squares changes the
one-step weight; it leaves the population zero restrictions unchanged. The code therefore
reports this estimator as scaled identity-weight GMM, not the canonical homoskedastic optimal
one-step estimator. Small objective values with many instruments can reflect overfitting. An
overidentification test is neither proof of exclusion nor evidence of adequate instrument strength.


8.9.2    A paired comparison and a banking decision rule

The synthetic short-panel experiment uses N = 800, eight transitions after an initial observation,
and yit = αi + ρyi,t−1 + .6xit + vit , with xit = .5xi,t−1 + .4vit + ηit . A 400-period burn-in
generates the regular initial law. The initial-condition challenger then adds a multiple of αi to
the initial balance; the serial-error challenger changes the innovation law. The four methods
use identical datasets. Coverage below is joint for both coefficients, using two-coordinate
Bonferroni 95% intervals across 400 repetitions.

               Regime                   Difference 1 Difference 2 System 1 System 2
               Stationary                      .955        .950        .958       .948
               Persistent                      .985        .983        .968       .933
               Initial departure               .950        .960        .033       .000
               Serial-error violation          .000        .000        .000       .000

One and two denote weighting steps, not different causal targets. Near 95% coverage, the
Monte Carlo standard error is about .011. The very high coverage of a weak differenced design
is not a precision advantage; weak moments can produce broad intervals and unreliable normal
approximations. The initial-departure failure is the decisive exclusion from an automatic
system-GMM default. For established comparable entities, system moments can be a challenger
after a substantive initial-law argument. For new portfolios, the primary differenced route has
the weaker initial-law requirement, but must still report Jacobian strength, instrument count
and residual serial correlation. If those fail, the result is an unsupported inferential claim, not
a prompt to search until a small standard error appears.
   Misspecification-robust moment inference is another distinct alternative. Kleibergen and
Zhan (2021, Sections 2–3, Assumptions 1–2) targets the minimizer of a continuously updated
population GMM criterion when no parameter makes all moments zero. Its joint moment/Jaco-
bian CLT and covariance conditions support an identification- and misspecification-robust score
construction. That pseudo-true minimizer need not equal a causal response or a meaningful
risk premium. This use of “double robust” concerns weak identification and moment misspeci-
fication; it is different from outcome/propensity robustness in Chapter 3. The inspected copy
is the 2021 preprint of work identified in 2025 journal metadata. It is a substantive inference
challenger, not a license to keep a causal label after the identifying restrictions fail.

8.10.1     What an exact synthetic-control inference route actually needs

Synthetic-control weights interpolate pre-intervention outcomes, usually under nonnegative
weights summing to one. Their value depends on pre-fit, factor balance, donor contamination
and whether the treated unit is inside the donor support (Abadie et al., 2010; Abadie, 2021;
Ben-Michael et al., 2021; Arkhangelsky et al., 2021). A fitted counterfactual curve is not a
confidence procedure by itself. Consider one precise banking design: one of J eligible regions
80                                                                   Causal analysis for a universal bank


is selected uniformly for a sustained pilot, after the eligibility set and fitting algorithm are
fixed. Under the sharp null of no effect in every post-period, the complete untreated outcome
matrix is invariant to this assignment.
  For each candidate treated region j, refit its donor weights using its own pre-period and
the remaining J − 1 regions. Apply the same fixed regularization and fit exclusions to every
candidate. Compute a discrepancy Tj , such as post-period mean squared gap divided by a
pre-period error with a fixed positive floor. With observed assignment a,
                                                 J
                                     pa = J −1
                                                 X
                                                       1{Tj ≥ Ta }
                                                 j=1

is super-uniform under the randomization: conditional on the fixed outcome matrix, a is uniform
over the J positions in its rank list. Ties make the displayed test conservative. Serial correlation,
common shocks and weight estimation do not invalidate this finite assignment argument because
the whole paths are held fixed and the fitting algorithm is applied symmetrically. Few eligible
regions impose coarse attainable significance.
   For a sharp constant additive effect τ in every post-period, subtract τ from the actual treated
path to impute the untreated matrix. For each possible assignment add the hypothesized
effect to that region, then recompute the discrepancy centered on τ , including its donor fit.
Inverting the resulting tests gives a confidence set for this sharp constant-effect model. It is
not automatically an interval for an arbitrary average treatment effect under heterogeneous
post-period effects.
   An observationally selected distressed bank is not uniformly randomized among healthy
donors. Its donor placebo ranks are then descriptive unless another exchangeability/design
argument is supplied. A residual-permutation or Bayesian structural time-series route substi-
tutes its own temporal or prior/model restrictions; neither inherits the assignment proof. This
is why the product selects the above test for randomized regional pilots and returns an explicit
additional-design requirement for observational donor studies. The method choice concerns
the source of uncertainty, not a claim that one donor-fitting algorithm is universally preferable.
   A stronger temporal challenger is the null-imposed conformal construction of Chernozhukov
et al. (2022c). It imputes the hypothesized untreated outcome, refits the counterfactual
prediction under that null, and ranks its residual discrepancy over a declared permutation
group. Exact validity follows under the required exchangeability and permutation-equivariant
fitting. For dependent observations, their Theorem 1 instead assumes a fixed postperiod length,
stationary mixing shocks with a bounded discrepancy density and small prediction errors
both on average and at the tested dates. Theorem 2 uses estimator stability plus a stationary
exponentially mixing data law. These are substantive ways to trade assignment information
for temporal prediction restrictions. Neither is a license to permute arbitrary nonstationary
bank residuals, and neither automatically changes a sharp path hypothesis into the mean effect
in Equation (8.11). For an observational regional rollout this challenger can be selected only
after its null prediction and temporal restrictions are defended. The randomized pilot route
was selected here because its source of repeated assignment is specified directly.
Chapter 9

Time series, structural shocks and
observation frequency

9.1     A temporal prediction is not yet a shock intervention
In treasury and deposit management, a bank may ask how a policy-rate shock changes balances
over the next year. In collections it may ask how repeated assistance changes repayment
along a customer trajectory. Both have time indices, but the interventions differ. A structural
macroeconomic shock perturbs one innovation while the system’s other mechanisms continue
to respond. A sustained policy replaces a sequence of decision rules. A forecast conditions on
observed historical values. These are different operations on a dynamic model.
   Let Xt be a vector of observed series and let Ft be their observed past. Granger noncausality
of series X j for X i is a restriction saying that removing the past of X j from the conditioning
information does not change the conditional law, or in its mean version the conditional mean,
of Xti . It is a property of a specified information set. It acquires an intervention interpretation
only under extra conditions on hidden causes, timing, instantaneous effects and structural
innovations (Peters et al., 2017, Chapter 10, Section 10.3).
   For a simple counterexample, let independent Ut cause Xt = Ut + ηt and Yt+1 = Ut + νt+1 ,
with independent noise. The past of X helps predict Y even though intervening on the
measurement Xt leaves Ut and Yt+1 unchanged. Conversely, an entirely instantaneous effect of
Xt on Yt with independent observations over time need not generate any predictive benefit
from lagged X. Neither failure is repaired by a more accurate nonlinear prediction model.

        mation

9.2.1    Non-Gaussianity adds information, with substantive costs

For the model Xt = B0 Xt + pℓ=1 Bℓ Xt−ℓ + εt , reduced lag matrices are (I − B0 )−1 Bℓ .
                                 P

Hyvärinen et al. (2010, Sections 2 and 5) uses mutually independent, non-Gaussian innovations
over components and time, and an acyclic instantaneous graph, to identify and estimate the
structural system. ICA identifies the innovation mixing up to its scale/permutation ambiguities,
and the acyclic structural restrictions resolve the appropriate normalization and ordering.
The assumptions add higher-order information beyond covariance. They also exclude latent
common causes in that model. Fat-tailed bank returns alone do not establish independent
structural innovations, and stochastic volatility can produce marginal non-Gaussianity with
shared dependence.
   The distinction between Bℓ and (I − B0 )−1 Bℓ explains why a reduced lag coefficient includes
instantaneous propagation. Reporting it as one direct structural edge can misstate both its size
and its mechanism. Non-Gaussian discovery is therefore a scientific identification route with
testable implications and untestable restrictions, not a preprocessing option for an otherwise
unidentified VAR.

9.3.1    Direct projections and VAR propagation

An LP-IV estimates a separate instrumented regression for each horizon. A proxy-SVAR first
recovers reduced innovations and dynamics, then identifies a structural impact column from
instrument–innovation covariances and propagates it. Under suitable invertibility, structural
shocks are recoverable from present and past observed innovations. That condition is additional
information about the observation system. The direct LP-IV argument above can identify a
response without a finite-order invertible VAR, but its lead/lag exclusion is strong. Under
different control-variable conditions the requirements of the two approaches can coincide (Stock
and Watson, 2018, Sections 2–3).
   A scalar illustration shows what noninvertibility loses. Let Xt = εt + θεt−1 with Gaussian
white noise of variance σ 2 and |θ| > 1. Its autocovariances are identical to those of the
invertible representation with coefficient 1/θ and innovation variance θ2 σ 2 : both have variance
(1 + θ2 )σ 2 and lag-one covariance θσ 2 . Higher-lag covariances vanish, so the Gaussian laws
agree. Their unit-impact structural responses at horizon one are nevertheless θ and 1/θ.
Choosing the invertible likelihood representation is a normalization of observable prediction;
calling its innovation the economic shock needs justification.
   LP estimators have more freedom across horizons; VAR propagation imposes restrictions
through powers of common lag matrices. This creates an estimation bias/variance comparison
after identification, not a theorem that direct projections always answer a causal question or
that VARs always have lower error. The constructions and inference alternatives are reviewed
by Jordà and Taylor (2024, Sections 2 and 6). Moreover, identifying the normalized response
does not automatically identify the shock’s variance, every historical shock realization, or its
share of forecast-error variance. Those require additional recoverability and normalization
information (Stock and Watson, 2018, Section 2.5).

Here the score CLT, covariance summability and a nondegenerate variance are imposed
conditions; stationarity alone does not imply them. Covariance estimation needs further
conditions; a kernel HAC estimator truncates weighted empirical lag covariances at a bandwidth
that grows suitably slowly with T . Specifying that estimator without stating its regime is not
an uncertainty guarantee.
   Multi-step regression errors often overlap in future innovations, but it is the instrument-
times-error score that controls inference. Under additional orthogonality, a lag-augmented
construction can yield serially uncorrelated scores even with overlapping regression errors. The
ordinary and augmented constructions therefore need different justifications; Jordà and Taylor
(2024, Sections 6.1–6.3) discusses these distinctions and the source-specific uniform results.
An arbitrary nonlinear LP with a learned instrument does not inherit them.
  Fitting nuisance functions on separate time blocks likewise requires a dependence argument.
Under absolute regularity, coupling a block to an independent version can have an error
controlled by the absolute-regularity coefficient at the separating gap. With many blocks, the
accumulated error must vanish. The gap must also account for an outcome that extends h
dates after its origin; disjoint origin dates can still share outcomes and innovations. Random
row splitting supplies neither control. A prospective evaluation additionally requires training
and features available at the historical decision date; an offline stationary-law cross-fitting
argument alone does not certify that prospective use.
   Joint inference across horizons needs the stacked score covariance, including cross-horizon
terms. A collection of pointwise 95% intervals is not a simultaneous 95% response band. Weak
normalization denominators, unit roots, structural breaks, growing horizons and heavy tails
can each change the limiting argument. The appropriate result may be an identified set,
a sensitivity analysis or a shorter supported horizon rather than a smooth but unjustified
response curve.


9.6     A complete stationary response experiment
The moment identity in Equation (9.2) becomes a usable operation only after specifying how
observations repeat. Consider a three-dimensional vector containing a policy rate, deposits
and lending, all in declared units. Let
                                                                                     q
            Xt = F Xt−1 + Bεt ,             Zt = aε1t + vt ,        vt = ρv vt−1 +       1 − ρ2v ζt .
The innovations are mutually independent standard Gaussian vectors/scalars; the joint process
starts in its stationary law. The eigenvalues of F and ρv have modulus below one, with a
fixed stability margin. The matrix B is nonsingular, B11 ̸= 0, and initially aB11 is bounded
away from zero. Gaussianity is a statistical restriction of this reference experiment, while the
instrument restrictions supply causal identification. The Gaussian observational VAR itself

9.6.1    Why a central limit theorem applies here

For this particular experiment the limiting argument can be reconstructed directly. The jointly
Gaussian vector process (Xt , Zt ) has geometrically decaying autocovariances and a bounded
spectral density. Gaussian moment pairing shows that the covariance of any two centered
quadratic products is a sum of products of two covariances. Hence the score covariances are
absolutely summable; a fixed horizon shift changes the constants, not summability.
   For any fixed vector c, collect the finitely many Gaussian observations needed for t c′ Mt
                                                                                              P

into Gn . That sum is a centered quadratic form G′n An Gn − tr(An Σn ). Each observation is
paired with only a fixed number of lags, so ∥An ∥ is bounded. Absolute covariance summability
                                                       1/2   1/2
bounds ∥Σn ∥ uniformly. The eigenvalues λnr of Σn An Σn are consequently bounded, and
the form has the law r λnr (χ21r − 1) with independent terms. Its variance divided by n
                        P

converges to c′ Ωc. If this limit is positive, the fourth-moment Lyapunov ratio is bounded by
C r λ4nr /( r λ2nr )2 = O(n−1 ). If the limit is zero, the normalized form converges to zero
  P        P

in L2 . Applying this argument to every c proves the joint Gaussian limit. With D̄ → q,

9.6.3    Weak instruments require a different result object

Do not divide by a weak normalization to construct the inferential pivot. For a proposed
response b, test the zero mean of Utj − bDt . Write SU U , SU D , SDD for the corresponding entries
of the Bartlett matrix of the centered joint products (Ut , Dt ). Accept b if

                            n(Ūj − bD̄)2 ≤ c2 (SU U − 2bSU D + b2 SDD ).                         (9.9)

This is one quadratic inequality Ab2 + Bb + C ≤ 0, with A = nD̄2 − c2 SDD , B = −2nŪj D̄ +
2c2 SU D , and C = nŪj2 − c2 SU U . Its solution can be an interval, two unbounded rays, the
whole line, an empty set, or a degenerate singleton/half-line. These cases must survive the
interface. At the true b, the score CLT does not require dividing by q, and remains applicable
along bounded weak-instrument sequences with a nondegenerate residual-score variance and
fixed stability margin. Bonferroni inversion across coordinates yields simultaneous coverage of
the true response vector. At q = 0 the normalized causal response is not identified by these
moments; a statistical set cannot repair that. No first-stage threshold is used to switch silently
between guarantees.

9.7      Learned controls under explicit temporal separation
Many bank analyses require hundreds of release-vintage controls. A partially linear IV model
supplies a precise learning target:

        Yt = θDt + g(Ct ) + et ,   E[et | Ct , Zt ] = 0,   (ℓ, r, m)(c) = E[(Yt , Dt , Zt ) | Ct = c].

The orthogonal score and its identifying slope are

     ψt (θ, η) = (Zt − m(Ct )){Yt − ℓ(Ct ) − θ[Dt − r(Ct )]},         J = E[(Zt − m)(Dt − r)] ̸= 0.

Instruments, controls and the outcome horizon must already satisfy the causal restrictions.
Good nuisance prediction does not supply them. For fitted errors ∆m, ∆ℓ, ∆r, conditional on
an independent training sample, direct expansion gives the exact mean remainder

                            E{ψ(θ, ηb) − ψ(θ, η)} = E[∆m(∆ℓ − θ∆r)].                                     (9.10)

The first-order terms have zero means by their respective conditional moment restrictions. This
connects the dynamic procedure to the orthogonality argument in Chapter 3 and Chernozhukov
et al. (2018), with a new sampling argument still needed.
   One sufficient construction is deliberately explicit. Suppose the underlying observables and
fitted functions are bounded, the process is absolutely regular with β(k) ≤ C exp(−ck), and
lag/horizon windows are fixed. Use two contiguous blocks of comparable size, separated by
g = ⌈3 log n/c⌉ after expanding both blocks for every feature lag and future outcome. Train
on either block and evaluate on the other. Absolute regularity couples the pair of blocks to
independent blocks with error at most C exp(−cg) = O(n−3 ). Both fits use this same coupled
pair; independence of the two fitted estimates is not asserted. An unknown c is a scientific
tuning uncertainty. The formula is a sufficient regime specification, not an estimate of c from
a few scores.
   Let δn bound the three population L2 nuisance errors. For a bounded centered score
difference its lag covariance is bounded both by Cδn2 and by C exp(−ck). Splitting the lag sum
at k ≍ log(1/δn ) bounds its long-run variance by Cδn2 {1 + log(1/δn )}. Conditional centering,
Chebyshev’s inequality and Equation (9.10) then give the oracle linearization when

                       δn → 0,       ∥∆m∥2 (∥∆ℓ∥2 + |θ|∥∆r∥2 ) = op (n−1/2 ).

The oracle CLT can also be constructed here. Split the bounded centered score into big
blocks of length m = ⌊n1/3 ⌋, separated by gaps b = ⌈C log n⌉ with cC > 2. Summable score
covariances bound the variance of the discarded gaps by a constant times their number of
observations, O(n2/3 log n) = o(n). Coupling the remaining big blocks to independent blocks
fails with probability at most O(n2/3 e−cb ) = o(1). Each centered block is bounded by O(m),
           √
which is o( n); hence the independent-block Lindeberg condition holds. Their variance divided
by n converges to the summable long-run variance. Cramér–Wold and the negligible gaps give
the vector CLT.
   For covariance estimation, a covariance of two score products decomposes into a fourth
cumulant plus two products of pairwise covariances. Bounded exponential absolute regularity
bounds the cumulant by an exponential in the largest separating gap of the four dates; summing
its possible gaps is finite. Pairwise terms are summable as well. This gives a uniform C/n
                                                                  √
variance bound for empirical lag covariances, and the same Op (L/ n) conservative stochastic
bound as above. Across the deleted central gap, do not pretend the two observed endpoints
are adjacent. Sum lag products within each evaluation block using the total retained length
9.7. Learned controls under explicit temporal separation                                       89


as denominator. The missing oracle boundary pairs contribute O(L2 /n), which vanishes for
L = ⌊n1/4 ⌋.
   There is an additional condition for fitted-score covariance. If the empirical root-mean-
square score error is rn , Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the difference of the two HAC matrices by
Op (Lrn + Lrn2 ). Take δn to be a deterministic high-probability bound on the population errors.
Conditional evaluation and Markov’s inequality applied to the mean squared score error give
rn = Op (δn ); the coupling failure probability vanishes. Require Lδn = o(1), as well as the
product condition. Taking all nuisance errors op (n−1/4 ) is sufficient for the stated bandwidth.
A maximum lag-covariance error op (1) alone cannot be summed over an increasing number of
lags.


9.7.1    When sparsity supplies the required rates

For a concrete learner suppose each conditional mean is a linear combination of p ≤ na
bounded, standardized features, with at most s nonzero coefficients, plus an explicitly controlled
approximation error. Assume a population restricted eigenvalue bounded below. Partition
training data into alternating blocks of length b = C0 log n, with C0 > (3 + 2a)/c. Coupling
alternate blocks, followed by bounded-block concentration
                                                p          and a union bound over scores and
Gram entries, gives deviations of order λn = C1 log n log(pn)/n for a constant C1 depending
on the envelope and dependence constants. This conservative penalty includes a logarithmic
dependence cost.
  The Lasso basic inequality on the event ∥n−1 Ct et ∥∞ ≤ λn /2 restricts its error to a cone.
                                                   P
                                                     √
Restricted curvature then gives prediction error Op ( sλn ) and coefficient ℓ1 error Op (sλn ).
Concentration of the Gram matrix transfers the empirical prediction bound to population L2
when sλn = o(1). Clipping predictions to the known outcome envelope cannot increase that
                                                   √
population error. Consequently s log n log(pn) = o( n), with approximation errors obeying
the same product and bandwidth restrictions, supplies a complete sufficient learning regime.
This is substantially stronger than merely p < n.
   Babii et al. (2020, Assumptions 3.1–3.4 and Theorem 3.1) develops a more flexible sparse-
group route under τ -mixing and polynomial tails, with a penalty depending explicitly on
moments and decay rates. Its prediction inequalities do not automatically supply the population
nuisance rates or the bounded coupling argument just used. A factor alternative Ct = Λft + eC    t
economizes on a dense common component, but dropping eC          t is valid adjustment only if the
omitted component has no remaining confounding role, or its bias is bounded. Sparsity and
factor reduction are therefore different scientific restrictions. Forecast RMSE does not decide
between them for causal inference.
   The current proposal of Ciganovic et al. (2026, Assumptions 2.1–2.5) uses reverse cross-fitting
for time series and explicitly assumes conditional plug-in stability. That assumption cannot be
deduced from disjoint row indices or reversibility. For example, a stationary Gaussian process
can be reversible and still have nonsummable long-memory covariances. Its Supplement S1’s
increasing-bandwidth argument also needs control of the accumulated fitted-score discrepancy.
We retain the source as a relevant 2026 alternative and use the stronger explicit separation and
rate construction above for the initial justified route. Removing gaps requires a learner-specific
stability proof.

9.9     Persistence, cointegration and the level target
An integrated balance series is economically plausible and falls outside the stable-level experi-
ment. For a VAR(1) with semisimple unit roots and stable remaining roots,

                         ∆Xt = (F − I)Xt−1 + Bεt = αβ ′ Xt−1 + Bεt .

The rank of F − I and the stationary error-correction combinations β ′ Xt describe long-run
comovement. They do not identify which innovation is a monetary, liquidity or credit-supply
shock. The latter still requires an instrument or another economic restriction.
  There is an identified stationary transformation for the fixed-horizon external-IV target.

9.10. Consequences for a large-scale time-series product                                              91


Under mean independence of ut from the innovations at all other dates, the score formed with
the future projection error is serially uncorrelated even when that error overlaps. Montiel Olea
and Plagborg-Møller (2020, Definition 1, Assumptions 1–3, Proposition 1) proves marginal
uniform inference for a specified VAR parameter space, with eighth moments, summable
innovation-product cumulants and scaled design nonsingularity. Near unit roots its horizon
condition is hT /T → 0. This theorem does not itself establish external-IV ratio inference or
simultaneous bands. We select the stationary-change IV route for the integrated structural
response and retain lag augmentation as the justified alternative for its stated reduced-form
projection target.
   A regime break is a third problem. Pooling two different F or impact columns can average
two economic mechanisms. A stationary transformation does not remove a changing causal
response. Segmented analyses require enough dates in each segment, a declared treatment of
estimated break locations and, if used, a separate selection-aware uncertainty argument. The
product must identify that unresolved regime instead of interpreting one pooled curve as a
stable banking mechanism.


9.10      Consequences for a large-scale time-series product
The reusable object should contain the intervention or shock definition, normalization, ob-
servation frequency/operator, allowed contemporaneous structure, latent information, valid
moments and sampling regime. The estimation layer can share lag construction, sparse regres-
sions, filtering and score reductions, but must preserve which restrictions identify a structural
response.
   For many series, sparse VARs, low-rank factors and shared nuisance learners impose different
approximation restrictions. Reducing compute by screening lag pairs can remove a necessary
adjustment path; reducing frequency can destroy identifiability; pooling countries can impose
a common mechanism that their policy regimes do not share. Scale is thus a joint scientific
and computational design question. The next chapter develops what causal discovery can
contribute before those restrictions are promoted into a fitted effect model.


9.11      A practical hierarchy for persistence and dependent in-
          ference
A treasury analyst can reasonably want a deposit response at horizons zero through twelve, a
simultaneous statement about that whole curve, and an answer robust to a weak monetary-
policy instrument. These are three requirements. Changing the covariance bandwidth addresses
dependence; changing to a reduced-form projection may change the target; neither action
establishes the instrument’s exclusion restriction.
  For the direct-IV route, stack the raw moments as

                 Ωe = (I − A)Ωu (I − A)′ ,         Ωu = (I − A)−1 Ωe (I − A)−T .

The residuals need not be white: a misspecified stable AR(1) prefilter can still be followed by

of the inverse norm.
   The implementation fits a VAR(1) to the score vector, estimates a residual Bartlett covariance
and uses linear solves for recolouring. It reports the prefilter radius and condition number and
refuses an unstable estimate. The three compared methods use the same origins, instruments,
normalization and test inversion. Only covariance construction changes. This preserves the
intervention while revealing the inferential sensitivity.

9.11.2    Lag augmentation and a distinct joint construction

For an AR(1), regress yt+h on (1, yt , yt−1 ). Partialling out yt−1 makes the effective regressor
the innovation in yt . Under the source’s strong innovation restrictions, the relevant score
covariance permits heteroskedasticity-robust inference without a generic residual HAC penalty.
Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2020, Definition 1, Assumptions 2–3 and Proposition 1)
establishes a marginal result over a specified persistence/root class and horizon-growth regime.
For four prespecified horizons, applying that result at level α/4 and the union bound supplies
a simultaneous route; it does not require independent horizon estimates.
   The scalar experiment uses horizons (1, 4, 8, 12), the Eicker–Huber–White regression co-
variance and that Bonferroni critical value. Joint 95% coverage is .920, .943 and .928 for
ρ = .8, .985, 1 respectively, across 400 repetitions. This is evidence for an AR reduced-form
response under its innovation law. It is not a comparison on the external-IV normalized target
in Equation (9.11). Uniform marginal validity also does not by itself permit a growing number
of horizons without controlling the accumulated error (Inoue et al., 2023).
   The instrument need not affect every date equally. In the inspected 2025 dynamic-LATE
preprint, conditional instrument independence, exclusion, monotonicity, partial first-stage
support and smooth response restrictions make a generalized Wald ratio a weighted marginal
effect for the responsive subpopulation (Casini et al., 2025, Assumptions 2.1–2.5 and Proposition
2.1). Its further claim of date-specific complier recovery needs deterministic complier status
and local smoothness/comparison assumptions (Casini et al., 2025, Assumptions 2.6–2.8).
Neither statement licenses an analyst to choose the dates with the strongest observed first
stage and use an ordinary full-sample interval. Selected subsamples change population weights
and require a separately justified selection-aware inferential argument.


9.11.3    Choosing a route for a bank’s actual clock and panel

Common shocks require aggregation of customer scores by calendar date; customer count
does not manufacture independent shock realizations. In a separate AR(.95) date-score mean
experiment, short-window HAC covers .500 at 800 dates and .560 at 2,000 dates; prefiltering
covers .918 and .958. This favorable result supports prefiltering for that score model, while
the curve comparison above prevents generalizing it to every response. With heavy tails, the
moment and covariance conditions need checking or a different robust sampling argument;
trimming a shock changes the target unless a retained-population estimand is specified.
   The wider method hierarchy follows restrictions, not a package ranking. Use direct external-
IV projections when a dated external source of variation and its exclusion are defensible.
A finite VAR or factor reduction buys precision and long-horizon propagation by imposing
dynamics and rank; compare it with the direct route on identical shock normalization. Use
lag-augmented projections for their justified reduced-form or separately identified structural
target. An error-correction model is appropriate when levels have economically justified
cointegrating restrictions; estimating rank and deterministic trends changes the inferential
problem and cannot inherit a stationary score theorem. Differences answer change effects, with
level responses reconstructed by cumulation under the maintained integration model. Mixed-
frequency state-space/MIDAS designs add a measurement and aggregation law: quarterly
output is not three identical monthly observations. The observation-clock and factor derivations
earlier in this chapter explain the added information and aliasing cost. Breaks require a declared
stable subperiod, a prespecified regime model or explicitly local effects; a full-sample mean
response can otherwise average incompatible policies.
  These alternatives are proposed supported model families, not automatically selected
94                                                                 Causal analysis for a universal bank


truths. The reusable response operation reports the stability, normalization, dependence and
aggregation premises, the primary estimate, a substantive challenger and their disagreement.
When no family is credible, it returns an exploratory curve or a sensitivity set with that
limitation. Large-scale reduction remains valuable, but it follows the scientific unit and target
instead of choosing them.


9.12      A bank funding decision with common shocks and learned
          controls
Consider a treasury desk changing the offered deposit rate for one month by ten basis points.
The target is the response of a fixed branch portfolio’s balance stock, followed by the change
in funding contribution over seven months. This is neither a sustained repricing policy nor
the response to an unlabelled reduced-form innovation. Future prices follow their natural rule.
The customer and competitor mechanisms are held fixed; equilibrium repricing by competitors
would require a different model.

where kh = N c(dh m − r1{h = 0}) and B0 = 100 is fixed. The higher rate also applies to
